children.name: Araneae
Salticidae
Phidippus
children.description: Phidippus is a genus of robust, colorful jumping spiders that are among the largest and most conspicuous jumping spiders in North America. These spiders are active daytime hunters with excellent vision, using their powerful legs to leap many times their body length to catch prey or escape danger. They're known for their chunky build, iridescent chelicerae (mouthparts), and often striking color patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phidippus jumping spiders are distinguished from other jumping spider genera by their relatively large size, stocky build, and prominent forward-facing eyes that give them excellent depth perception. Many species also have distinctively colorful, metallic-looking mouthparts that can be bright green, blue, or red.
children.funFact: These spiders have some of the best color vision in the animal kingdom and can see into the ultraviolet spectrum, which helps them spot prey and communicate with potential mates through colorful displays.

children.name: Habronattus
children.description: Paradise jumping spiders are small, active hunters known for their incredible acrobatic abilities and elaborate courtship displays. These tiny spiders can leap many times their body length to catch prey or escape danger, using their excellent eyesight to judge distances perfectly. Males are particularly famous for their colorful ornaments and intricate dance moves used to woo potential mates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jumping spiders, paradise jumping spiders are distinguished by their particularly ornate male courtship displays, often featuring iridescent colors, decorative leg fringes, and complex choreographed movements. They tend to be smaller and more delicately built than many of their jumping spider relatives.
children.funFact: Male paradise jumping spiders perform some of the most elaborate courtship dances in the animal kingdom, with each species having its own signature moves - some wave colorful leg ornaments like flags, while others vibrate their abdomens or perform intricate zigzag patterns to impress females.

children.name: Pelegrina
children.description: Pelegrina is a genus of small jumping spiders known for their excellent vision and hunting abilities. These tiny predators are active during the day and use their keen eyesight to stalk and pounce on prey rather than building webs to catch food. They're commonly found on plants, tree bark, and other surfaces where they hunt for small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pelegrina jumping spiders are typically small and often display distinctive color patterns, including white markings on their faces or bodies, and sometimes bright yellow or orange coloration on their legs. They can be distinguished from other jumping spider genera by their specific eye arrangements and body proportions.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, Pelegrina jumping spiders have vision that's among the sharpest in the spider world and can spot potential prey or threats from distances many times their own body length.

children.name: Attulus
children.description: Attulus is a genus of small jumping spiders that are active hunters, using their excellent eyesight to spot and pounce on prey rather than building webs. These compact spiders are known for their ability to leap many times their body length when hunting or escaping danger. They are commonly found in various habitats from gardens and walls to flowers and sandy areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Attulus jumping spiders are typically smaller and more compact than many other jumping spider genera, with relatively short legs and stocky bodies. They often have distinctive markings or coloration patterns that help distinguish the various species.
children.funFact: The Flower Jumping Spider (Attulus floricola) is often found hunting on blooms where it ambushes other insects that come to feed on nectar, essentially turning flowers into hunting platforms.

children.name: Tutelina
children.description: Tutelina is a genus of small jumping spiders known for their ant-like appearance and behavior. These tiny spiders are excellent mimics, often resembling ants so closely that they can move among ant colonies without being detected. All members of this genus are relatively small and share similar body proportions and coloration patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tutelina jumping spiders are distinguished from other jumping spider genera by their elongated, narrow bodies and constricted waists that give them their characteristic ant-like appearance. They also tend to wave their front legs like antennae when walking, further enhancing their ant mimicry.
children.funFact: Some Tutelina species are such convincing ant mimics that they can actually live alongside real ant colonies, gaining protection from predators while hunting for small prey in the same areas where ants forage.

children.name: Marpissa
children.description: Marpissa is a genus of slender jumping spiders known for their elongated bodies and excellent vision. These small predators are active hunters that stalk their prey rather than building webs, using their powerful hind legs to leap surprising distances when capturing insects or escaping danger.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jumping spiders, Marpissa species have notably slender, elongated abdomens and tend to be more muted in coloration. They often have distinctive striped or lined patterns running along their bodies, as seen in species like the Four-lined Slender Jumping Spider.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'slender' jumping spiders, Marpissa species can jump more than 10 times their own body length, making them incredibly efficient micro-predators in New England's forests and gardens.

children.name: Eris
children.description: Eris is a genus of small jumping spiders known for their compact, robust bodies and excellent vision. These athletic little hunters are active during the day and use their keen eyesight to stalk prey rather than building webs. All three New England species are woodland dwellers that can often be found on tree bark, logs, and low vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eris jumping spiders are distinguished from other jumping spider genera by their relatively short, stocky legs and their habit of holding their front legs close to their body when at rest. They also tend to be less colorful than many other jumping spiders, typically displaying earth-tone patterns that help them blend with bark and dead leaves.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny spiders, Eris species can jump more than 10 times their own body length to catch prey or escape danger, using hydraulic pressure in their legs like little eight-legged rockets!

children.name: Hentzia
children.description: Long-jawed jumping spiders in the genus Hentzia are small, agile hunters known for their proportionally elongated chelicerae (jaws) compared to other jumping spiders. These tiny spiders are active predators that use their excellent vision and jumping ability to hunt small insects and other prey. They're typically found on vegetation, tree bark, and around human structures where they can ambush their quarry.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most notable feature of Hentzia spiders is their elongated jaws, which are much longer relative to their body size than those of most other jumping spider genera. Males often have particularly prominent, forward-projecting chelicerae that they use in courtship displays.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting large jaws, these spiders are actually quite small - most Hentzia species have body lengths of only 3-5 millimeters, making their 'long' jaws still smaller than a grain of rice!

children.name: Pseudeuophrys
children.description: Pseudeuophrys is a genus of small jumping spiders known for their compact bodies and excellent vision. These tiny hunters are active predators that stalk and pounce on their prey rather than building webs to catch food. Both New England species are commonly found around human dwellings and other structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other jumping spiders by their relatively small size and specific patterns of coloration on their bodies and legs. They typically have darker, more muted colors compared to some of the more brightly colored jumping spider genera.
children.funFact: Despite being called "jumping" spiders, Pseudeuophrys species are actually more likely to slowly stalk their prey and make short, precise leaps rather than making dramatic long-distance jumps.

children.name: Zygoballus
children.description: Zygoballus is a genus of small jumping spiders known for their exceptional eyesight and hunting abilities. These compact spiders are active predators that stalk their prey rather than building webs, using their powerful legs to leap several times their body length to catch insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their relatively robust build compared to other jumping spiders, with males often displaying distinctive jaw modifications or enlarged chelicerae that give some species their common names.
children.funFact: The Hammer-jawed Jumping Spider gets its name from the male's dramatically enlarged and modified jaws, which are used in courtship displays and male-to-male combat over territory and mates.

children.name: Colonus
children.description: Colonus is a small genus of jumping spiders found in wooded areas across North America. These compact spiders are known for their excellent eyesight and ability to leap several times their body length to catch prey or escape danger. Like all jumping spiders, they actively hunt during the day rather than building webs to catch their food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Colonus jumping spiders are distinguished by their relatively robust build and preference for tree bark and wooden surfaces where their mottled coloration provides excellent camouflage. They tend to be less colorful than many other jumping spider genera, with earth-tone patterns that help them blend into their forest habitat.
children.funFact: The Sylvan Jumping Spider gets its name from the Latin word 'silva' meaning forest, reflecting its strong preference for woodland environments where it spends most of its time hunting on tree trunks and fallen logs.

children.name: Synageles
children.description: Synageles is a small genus of jumping spiders known for their remarkable ability to mimic ants in both appearance and behavior. These tiny spiders have evolved elongated body shapes and distinctive movement patterns that help them blend in with ant colonies. Both New England species are quite small and can be challenging to spot due to their excellent mimicry.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jumping spiders, Synageles species have noticeably constricted abdomens and often hold their front legs up like antennae while walking in jerky, ant-like movements.
children.funFact: These spiders are such convincing ant mimics that they can actually live among real ant colonies, gaining protection from predators who avoid the aggressive ants they're imitating.

children.name: Admestina
children.description: Admestina is a small genus of tiny parasitoid wasps that specialize in attacking other insects. These miniature wasps are part of the chalcid wasp family and play an important role as natural pest controllers in forest and garden ecosystems. Both New England species are quite small and can be challenging to spot without magnification.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Admestina can be distinguished from other chalcid wasps by their specific wing venation patterns and distinctive body proportions. They have relatively robust bodies compared to many other tiny parasitoid wasps.
children.funFact: Despite being smaller than many ants, Admestina wasps are skilled hunters that can precisely locate their host insects using chemical cues, making them incredibly effective biological control agents.

children.name: Platycryptus
children.description: Platycryptus is a small genus of jumping spiders known for their relatively large size and distinctive flat appearance. These spiders are excellent hunters that rely on their keen eyesight and powerful jumping ability to catch prey rather than building webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their flattened body shape and relatively large size compared to other jumping spiders. They typically have a mottled brown and tan coloration that provides excellent camouflage against tree bark.
children.funFact: Despite being called jumping spiders, Platycryptus spiders are actually more likely to run quickly across surfaces than to make dramatic leaps, earning them the nickname 'running jumping spiders.'

children.name: Salticus
children.description: Salticus is a genus of jumping spiders known for their bold black and white striped patterns and excellent eyesight. These small spiders are active hunters that stalk their prey rather than building webs, using their powerful legs to leap distances many times their body length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Salticus are distinguished from other jumping spiders by their distinctive zebra-like striping pattern and their preference for hunting on vertical surfaces like walls and tree trunks.
children.funFact: Salticus spiders have some of the best color vision in the spider world and can see into the ultraviolet spectrum, helping them spot prey and potential mates.

children.name: Maevia
children.description: Maevia is a genus of jumping spiders known for their exceptional sexual dimorphism, where males and females look dramatically different from each other. These small, active hunters are part of the jumping spider family and are known for their excellent eyesight and ability to leap several times their body length to catch prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Males of this genus are particularly notable for having two distinct color forms - a gray form and a more colorful form with iridescent scales and ornate leg decorations used in courtship displays.
children.funFact: Male Maevia spiders perform elaborate courtship dances with different choreography depending on which of their two color forms they possess - the flashy males wave their decorated front legs like semaphore flags, while the gray males use more subtle movements.

children.name: Naphrys
children.description: Naphrys is a small genus of jumping spiders known for their compact, robust build and excellent jumping abilities. These tiny spiders are active hunters that use their keen eyesight and powerful legs to leap onto prey rather than building webs to catch food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Naphrys jumping spiders are distinguished by their particularly stout, thick-bodied appearance compared to other jumping spider genera, giving them an almost chunky or compact look.
children.funFact: The only New England species, Naphrys pulex, gets its common name 'flea jumping spider' because of its small size and incredible ability to jump distances many times its own body length, much like a flea.

children.name: Paraphidippus
children.description: Paraphidippus is a small genus of jumping spiders found primarily in North America. These are medium-sized jumping spiders known for their robust build and excellent vision, like all members of the jumping spider family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their relatively large size compared to other jumping spiders and their distinctive coloration patterns, often featuring bright golden or orange hues.
children.funFact: The Golden Jumping Spider in this genus gets its name from the brilliant golden-orange coloration of males, making them one of the most colorful jumping spiders in New England.

children.name: Synemosyna
children.description: Synemosyna is a genus of jumping spiders that are masters of disguise, perfectly mimicking ants in both appearance and behavior. These tiny spiders have evolved elongated bodies and modified front legs that they wave like antennae to fool both predators and prey into thinking they're harmless ants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jumping spiders with compact, rounded bodies, Synemosyna species have distinctly narrow, elongated abdomens and constricted waists that closely resemble an ant's three-part body structure.
children.funFact: These spiders are so convincing in their ant mimicry that they often walk among real ant colonies without being detected, even fooling experienced entomologists at first glance!

children.name: Evarcha
children.description: Evarcha is a genus of jumping spiders known for their excellent vision and hunting abilities. These small, agile spiders are active predators that stalk and pounce on their prey rather than building webs to catch food. They have compact, robust bodies and are often found in sunny, open habitats where they can easily spot potential meals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Evarcha jumping spiders can be distinguished from other jumping spider genera by their relatively stocky build and specific eye arrangement. They typically have a more rounded carapace (front body section) compared to the more elongated forms seen in some other jumping spider groups.
children.funFact: Evarcha jumping spiders have some of the best color vision in the spider world, with four types of color receptors that allow them to see into the ultraviolet spectrum - better color vision than most mammals!

children.name: Hakka
children.description: Hakka is a genus of marine bryozoans, which are tiny colonial animals that build intricate, lace-like structures on rocks and other surfaces in the ocean. These filter-feeding creatures create colonies made up of hundreds of microscopic individuals called zooids, each living in its own small chamber. They play an important role in marine ecosystems by filtering plankton from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hakka bryozoans are distinguished by their distinctive colony architecture and the specific shape and arrangement of their zooid chambers. The genus is relatively rare and has unique skeletal features that separate it from other bryozoan groups.
children.funFact: Despite being animals, bryozoan colonies like Hakka often get mistaken for plants or corals because of their branching, tree-like growth patterns.

children.name: Phlegra
children.description: Phlegra is a genus of jumping spiders known for their compact, robust bodies and distinctive hunting behaviors. These small spiders are active predators that use their excellent eyesight to stalk and pounce on prey rather than building webs to catch food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phlegra jumping spiders can be distinguished from other jumping spider genera by their relatively short, stocky build and their tendency to hunt close to the ground on rocks, logs, and low vegetation.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, Phlegra jumping spiders have some of the best color vision in the animal kingdom and can see into the ultraviolet spectrum, helping them spot prey and potential mates.

children.name: Myrmarachne
children.description: Ant-mimic spiders are remarkable jumping spiders that have evolved to look and behave like ants. They have elongated bodies, constricted waists, and often hold their front legs up like antennae to complete their disguise. These clever spiders move in jerky, ant-like motions to fool both predators and prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other jumping spiders, Myrmarachne have distinctly narrow, elongated abdomens and a constricted waist that mimics an ant's three-part body structure. They also have enlarged front sections that resemble an ant's head and thorax.
children.funFact: These spiders are such convincing mimics that they can walk among real ant colonies without being detected, sometimes even stealing food from the ants they're impersonating!

children.name: Neon
children.description: Neon is a genus of tiny jumping spiders known for their miniature size and active hunting behavior. These spiders are among the smallest jumping spiders you'll encounter, but they still possess the characteristic excellent eyesight and athletic jumping abilities that define their family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Neon spiders are distinguished from other jumping spiders by their extremely small size and relatively simple, less colorful appearance compared to their flashier relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that they could easily sit on the head of a pin, Neon jumping spiders still perform the elaborate courtship dances and displays that jumping spiders are famous for.

children.name: Euophrys
children.description: Euophrys is a genus of small jumping spiders known for their excellent vision and ability to leap many times their body length to catch prey. These tiny hunters are active during the day and use their keen eyesight to stalk insects rather than building webs to trap them. They're part of the large jumping spider family, which includes some of the most agile and intelligent spiders in the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Euophrys spiders are distinguished from other jumping spiders by their relatively small size and specific eye arrangements, with four large front-facing eyes that give them exceptional depth perception for hunting.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, Euophrys spiders can jump up to 50 times their own body length with pinpoint accuracy to pounce on unsuspecting prey.

children.name: Talavera
children.description: Talavera is a genus of very small jumping spiders known for their tiny size and active hunting behavior. These spiders are visual hunters that use their excellent eyesight to stalk and pounce on prey rather than building webs to catch food. They are part of the diverse jumping spider family, which includes some of the most athletic and agile spiders in the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Talavera spiders are distinguished by their extremely small size, even among jumping spiders, and their distinctive eye arrangement with large forward-facing eyes. They have a compact, robust body shape and are often found in ground-level habitats rather than on vegetation.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny enough to sit comfortably on a pencil eraser, Talavera spiders have proportionally enormous eyes that give them vision rivaling that of much larger predators.

children.name: Chinattus
children.description: Chinattus is a small genus of jumping spiders found in mountainous regions of North America. These tiny spiders are specialized hunters that use their excellent eyesight and jumping abilities to catch prey much larger than themselves. They are part of the diverse jumping spider family, known for their active hunting style rather than building webs to catch food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chinattus jumping spiders are distinguished by their extremely small size and preference for high-altitude rocky habitats. They have proportionally large front-facing eyes and compact bodies adapted for life in harsh mountain environments.
children.funFact: Despite being among the smallest jumping spiders in North America, Chinattus spiders can leap distances many times their own body length to capture prey or escape danger.

children.name: Peckhamia
children.description: Peckhamia is a small genus of jumping spiders known for their exceptional eyesight and acrobatic hunting abilities. These tiny predators are active hunters that stalk their prey rather than building webs, using their powerful legs to leap many times their body length to capture insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Peckhamia spiders can be distinguished from other jumping spiders by their relatively small size and specific patterns of coloration and markings on their bodies and legs.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, Peckhamia spiders have some of the best vision in the spider world, with their large front-facing eyes providing sharp, color vision that rivals that of much larger animals.

children.name: Attidops
children.description: Attidops is a small genus of jumping spiders that belongs to the diverse family Salticidae. These tiny arachnids are characterized by their excellent eyesight and ability to leap many times their body length to catch prey or escape danger. Like other jumping spiders, they actively hunt during the day rather than building webs to trap insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Attidops spiders are distinguished from other jumping spider genera by their relatively small size and specific arrangement of eyes and body proportions. They have a compact, robust build that sets them apart from the more elongated jumping spider species.
children.funFact: Despite being incredibly small, Attidops spiders have some of the sharpest vision in the animal kingdom relative to their size, with their principal eyes providing resolution that rivals much larger predators.

children.name: Plexippus
children.description: Housefly Catchers are a genus of jumping spiders known for their exceptional hunting abilities and preference for catching flies and other small flying insects. These spiders are excellent jumpers with keen eyesight, using their athletic prowess to pounce on prey rather than building webs to catch food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their robust build, relatively large size compared to other jumping spiders, and their distinctive eye arrangement with particularly prominent front-facing eyes that give them excellent depth perception for hunting.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Housefly Catchers,' these spiders are so effective at pest control that a single individual can catch and eat dozens of flies, mosquitoes, and other bothersome insects in just one day.

children.name: Ghelna
children.description: Ghelna is a small genus of moths in the family Geometridae, commonly known as geometer moths or inchworms. These moths are characterized by their delicate wings and the caterpillar stage that moves in a distinctive looping motion, appearing to measure the ground as they crawl.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ghelna moths can be distinguished from other geometer moths by their specific wing patterns and coloration. The genus has relatively few species compared to other groups in the same family.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Ghelna moths are called 'inchworms' because they lack middle legs and must arch their bodies to move forward, creating the illusion that they're measuring distances inch by inch.

children.description: Jumping spiders are a diverse family of small, active hunters known for their incredible eyesight and acrobatic hunting style. Rather than building webs to catch prey, these spiders actively stalk and pounce on insects, using their powerful hind legs to leap distances many times their body length. With their compact, robust bodies and often colorful patterns, they're among the most charismatic spiders you'll encounter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Jumping spiders can be identified by their exceptional forward-facing eyes - they have four large eyes arranged in a square pattern on their face, giving them better vision than most other spiders. Their compact, stocky build and tendency to move in quick, jerky motions also sets them apart from web-building spiders.
children.funFact: Some male jumping spiders perform elaborate courtship dances, waving their colorful legs and body parts in species-specific patterns to impress females - and they can see in color to appreciate these displays!

children.name: Araneidae
Araneus
children.description: The Araneus genus includes some of New England's most recognizable spiders, known for building the classic circular orb webs we often see spanning between branches and garden plants. These medium to large-sized spiders have distinctively rounded or angular abdomens and are skilled architects of symmetrical, wheel-like webs that they use to catch flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Araneus spiders can be identified by their bulbous, often colorfully patterned abdomens and their preference for building large, vertical orb webs in open spaces between vegetation. Unlike some other orbweavers, they typically have more robust bodies and often display intricate markings or cross-like patterns on their abdomens.
children.funFact: The Barn Orbweaver (Araneus cavaticus) gained literary fame as Charlotte in E.B. White's beloved children's book 'Charlotte's Web,' making it one of the most famous spiders in American literature.

children.name: Mastophora
children.description: American Bolas Spiders are remarkable arachnids that have abandoned traditional web-building in favor of a unique hunting strategy. Instead of spinning webs to catch prey, these spiders create a single sticky line with a glob of adhesive at the end, which they swing like a lasso or bolas to snare flying insects. They are typically small to medium-sized spiders with rounded abdomens and are most active at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb weavers, bolas spiders don't build traditional webs but instead use a single sticky capture line that they actively swing at prey. They also have the unique ability to produce chemical mimics of moth pheromones to lure their specific prey closer.
children.funFact: Bolas spiders are master chemical mimics - each species produces fake moth pheromones that perfectly match those of their preferred prey species, essentially catfishing moths into flying within striking distance of their sticky lasso.

children.name: Neoscona
children.description: Spotted Orbweavers are medium-sized spiders that build classic circular webs with sticky spiral threads to catch flying insects. These nocturnal hunters typically construct their webs in the evening and take them down by morning, often eating the silk to recycle the protein. They're commonly found in gardens, forests, and fields throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orbweavers, Neoscona spiders have distinctive spotted or mottled patterns on their abdomens and often show a folium (leaf-like marking) down the center. They also tend to remove their webs during daylight hours and hide in nearby vegetation, while many other orbweavers leave their webs up continuously.
children.funFact: These spiders can eat their entire web in just a few minutes each morning, recycling up to 90% of the silk proteins to build a fresh web the next evening.

children.name: Mangora
children.description: Mangora is a genus of small to medium-sized orb weaver spiders that build classic circular webs to catch flying insects. These spiders are typically compact and stocky, with relatively short legs compared to other orb weavers. They're commonly found in gardens, fields, and forest edges throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mangora spiders can be recognized by their relatively short, thick legs and compact body shape, which sets them apart from the longer-legged orb weavers in related genera. Many species also have distinctive color patterns or leg markings that help with identification.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, Mangora spiders are efficient hunters that can capture prey much larger than themselves in their perfectly geometric webs.

children.name: Micrathena
children.description: Micrathena spiders are distinctive orb weavers known for their spiky, angular body shapes that make them look like tiny medieval shields or arrowheads. These small to medium-sized spiders build classic circular webs to catch flying insects. The females are much larger than males and display the characteristic spiny abdomens that give many species their common names.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb weavers, Micrathena spiders have hard, sculptured abdomens with prominent spines, tubercles, or pointed projections that create their distinctive geometric shapes. Their bodies often appear more like plant thorns or seed pods than typical spiders.
children.funFact: The elaborate spines and bumps on Micrathena spiders aren't just for show - they likely help camouflage the spider as a piece of plant debris or make them harder for birds to swallow.

children.name: Larinioides
children.description: Furrow spiders are a small genus of orb weaver spiders that build the classic circular, spoke-like webs we often see in gardens and around buildings. These medium-sized spiders are known for their intricate web-building skills and their habit of sitting at the center of their webs waiting for prey. All three New England species are skilled hunters that help control flying insect populations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Furrow spiders can be distinguished from other orb weavers by their relatively stocky build and distinctive abdominal patterns, often featuring folium (leaf-like) markings or cross-shaped designs. They also tend to build their webs in more exposed locations than many other orb weaver species.
children.funFact: The Furrow Orbweaver gets its name from the distinctive furrow or groove that runs down the middle of its abdomen, giving it a unique sculptured appearance among orb weavers.

children.name: Argiope
children.description: Garden orbweavers are large, colorful spiders that build impressive circular webs in gardens, fields, and sunny open areas. These eye-catching arachnids are among the most recognizable spiders in New England, known for their distinctive black and yellow markings and substantial size.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Garden orbweavers can be identified by their large size, bold yellow and black coloration, and the distinctive zigzag pattern (called a stabilimentum) they weave into the center of their webs.
children.funFact: Female garden orbweavers often eat their webs each morning and rebuild them daily, recycling the silk proteins to conserve energy.

children.name: Cyclosa
children.description: Trashline Orbweavers are spiders that create distinctive circular webs decorated with a unique vertical line of debris down the center. They deliberately collect bits of prey remains, shed skins, and other small debris to create this "trashline" that runs through the hub of their web. These small to medium-sized spiders are masters of camouflage, often sitting motionless in their decorated webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb weavers, Cyclosa spiders build a distinctive vertical stabilimentum (web decoration) made of accumulated trash and debris. They also have the unique behavior of sitting directly on this trashline, making them incredibly difficult to spot.
children.funFact: The spider often positions itself right on the trashline and remains so perfectly still that it looks like just another piece of debris, fooling both predators and prey.

children.name: Hypsosinga
children.description: Hypsosinga is a genus of small to medium-sized orb weaver spiders that build classic circular webs to catch flying insects. These spiders are typically found in grassy areas, meadows, and garden spaces throughout New England, where they construct their webs among vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hypsosinga spiders can be recognized by their relatively small size and the placement of their orb webs close to the ground in grassy or low shrubby areas, unlike many other orb weavers that build webs higher up in trees or bushes.
children.funFact: The Rubens Orbweaver gets its name from its reddish coloration that resembles the warm tones found in paintings by the famous Flemish artist Peter Paul Rubens.

children.name: Araniella
children.description: Cucumber Spiders are small, bright green orb weavers that blend perfectly with the leaves and stems of plants. These tiny spiders build delicate circular webs to catch flying insects, and their vibrant green coloration helps them hide from both predators and prey. They are most active during the warmer months when vegetation is lush.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other orb weavers which are brown or gray, Cucumber Spiders are distinctively bright green with a rounded, almost spherical abdomen. Their small size and leaf-green coloration make them easily recognizable among New England's web-building spiders.
children.funFact: Despite their name, Cucumber Spiders get their moniker not from eating cucumbers, but from their bright green color that resembles a tiny cucumber!

children.name: Gea
children.description: Gea is a genus of orb weaver spiders known for building distinctive circular webs with geometric patterns. These spiders are part of the large family of orb weavers that create the classic wheel-shaped webs we often see in gardens and forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the genus Gea are distinguished by their ability to construct webs with distinctive heptagonal (seven-sided) sectors, giving their webs a more geometric appearance than typical circular orb webs.
children.funFact: The Heptagonal Orbweaver gets its name from the seven-sided geometric pattern it creates in its web, making it one of the most mathematically precise web builders in the spider world.

children.name: Eustala
children.description: Eustala is a genus of orb weaver spiders known for their distinctive body shape and web-building behavior. These spiders construct the classic circular webs with radiating spokes that we often associate with spider webs, though they may modify or abandon their webs more frequently than some other orb weavers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Eustala are characterized by their humped or angular abdomens, which give them their common name of 'humpbacked orbweavers.' They typically have relatively short, stout bodies compared to other orb weaver genera.
children.funFact: Humpbacked orbweavers often sit at the center of their webs with their front legs extended forward and back legs stretched behind them, creating a distinctive cross-like silhouette.

children.name: Acanthepeira
children.description: Star-bellied Orb-web Spiders are a small group of orb weavers known for the distinctive star-like patterns on their abdomens. These spiders build classic circular webs with sticky spiral threads to catch flying insects. They are medium-sized spiders that are most active during late summer and fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The star or cross-shaped markings on their rounded abdomens make them easily recognizable among orb weavers. They also tend to have more robust, stockier bodies compared to many other orb weaver species.
children.funFact: The Starbellied Orbweaver often sits in the center of its web with its legs positioned to form an 'X' shape, making it look like a living extension of the star pattern on its abdomen.

children.name: Metepeira
children.description: Metepeira is a genus of orb weaver spiders known for building distinctive webs with intricate, maze-like patterns. These medium-sized spiders are skilled architects that create complex geometric webs to catch flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical orb weavers with simple circular webs, Metepeira spiders add dense, labyrinthine tangles of silk threads above and around their webs, creating a three-dimensional trap.
children.funFact: The labyrinth orbweaver gets its name from the confusing maze of silk threads it weaves around its web, which helps disorient prey and makes escape nearly impossible once an insect gets trapped.

children.name: Aculepeira
children.description: Aculepeira is a genus of orb weaver spiders known for building classic circular webs with sticky spiral threads to catch flying insects. These spiders are typically medium-sized with rounded abdomens and are often found in rocky or woodland habitats. They belong to the large family of orb weavers, which includes many of the most recognizable web-building spiders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Aculepeira can be distinguished from other orb weavers by their preference for building webs in rocky crevices and cliff faces rather than in vegetation. They also tend to have more muted, earth-toned coloration that helps them blend in with their rocky surroundings.
children.funFact: The name Aculepeira literally means 'sharp-pointed,' referring to the pointed projections often found on their abdomens that help them camouflage against rocky surfaces.

children.name: Acacesia
children.description: Acacesia is a small genus of orb weaver spiders known for their distinctive angular, triangular body shape that resembles a leaf or thorn. These spiders build typical orb webs but have evolved a unique body form that helps them blend in with vegetation. They are relatively uncommon spiders that prefer wooded habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Acacesia spiders are easily recognized by their sharply pointed, triangular abdomen that comes to distinct points on either side, giving them an almost geometric appearance that's unlike most other orb weavers.
children.funFact: The Difoliate Orbweaver gets its name from the two leaf-like projections on its abdomen, which help it perfectly mimic a dead leaf when it sits motionless in its web.

children.name: Gasteracantha
children.description: Spiny Orbweavers are distinctive spiders known for their hard, shell-like abdomens covered in prominent spines or spikes. These small but eye-catching arachnids build circular webs like other orbweavers, but their armored appearance makes them look more like tiny crabs than typical spiders. They are among the most recognizable spiders due to their unique defensive spines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orbweaver spiders, Spiny Orbweavers have hard, heavily armored abdomens with sharp spines projecting from the sides and rear. Their compact, crab-like shape and protective spines make them unmistakable among New England's web-building spiders.
children.funFact: The spines on their abdomen serve as protection from predators - birds and other animals are less likely to attack something that looks so prickly and indigestible!

children.name: Mecynogea
children.description: Mecynogea is a genus of orb weaver spiders known for building distinctive circular webs with sticky spiral threads to catch flying insects. These spiders are part of the large orb weaver family and are skilled web architects that reconstruct their intricate traps regularly.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mecynogea spiders can be identified by their unique web design that often features a distinctive stabilimentum (zigzag silk decoration) and their habit of positioning themselves at the center or edge of their webs in a characteristic pose.
children.funFact: The Basilica Orbweaver gets its name from the ornate, cathedral-like appearance of its web, which can span up to 2 feet across and is often built in the same location night after night.

children.name: Ocrepeira
children.description: Ocrepeira is a small genus of orb weaver spiders known for building circular webs to catch flying insects. These spiders are part of the large orb weaver family and are typically found in wooded areas where they construct their webs between trees and shrubs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ocrepeira spiders can be distinguished from other orb weavers by their distinctive abdominal patterns and web-building behavior, often creating webs with fewer radial threads than many of their relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being orb weavers, some Ocrepeira species are known to occasionally abandon their webs and hunt actively, making them more versatile predators than many of their web-bound cousins.

children.name: Cercidia
children.description: Cercidia is a small genus of orb weaver spiders known for their vibrant coloration and distinctive web-building behavior. These spiders are part of the larger orb weaver family and create the classic circular webs that many people associate with spiders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cercidia spiders are distinguished by their bright red and orange coloration, which is relatively uncommon among orb weavers. They also have a more compact, rounded abdomen compared to many of their relatives.
children.funFact: The Carmine Orbweaver gets its name from its striking carmine red coloration, making it one of the most colorful spiders you might encounter in a New England garden.

children.name: Verrucosa
children.description: Verrucosa is a genus of orb weaver spiders known for their distinctive triangular abdomens covered in bumps and spines. These spiders build the classic circular webs we often associate with orb weavers, but their bodies have a unique sculptural appearance that sets them apart from their smoother relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Verrucosa can be identified by their distinctly triangular, flattened abdomens that are covered in warty bumps and small spines, giving them an almost armored appearance compared to other orb weavers.
children.funFact: The name 'Verrucosa' literally means 'warty' in Latin, referring to the bumpy texture of these spiders' abdomens that helps them blend in with tree bark and lichen when they're not on their webs.

children.description: Orbweavers are the classic spiders that build the circular, spoke-and-spiral webs we often see stretched between plants or structures. These spiders are master architects, creating intricate geometric webs to catch flying insects. Most orbweavers have rounded abdomens and relatively long legs, and they typically sit in the center of their web or hide nearby, waiting to feel the vibrations of trapped prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other web-building spiders, orbweavers construct the distinctive circular webs with radiating spokes and spiral capture threads. Many species rebuild their entire web daily, often eating the old silk to recycle the protein.
children.funFact: Some orbweavers, like the bolas spiders, have abandoned web-building entirely and instead swing a sticky ball of silk on a line to catch moths, mimicking the chemical scents that attract male moths to females.

children.name: Linyphiidae
Walckenaeria
children.description: Walckenaeria is a genus of tiny sheet web weaver spiders that are among the smallest spiders you'll encounter in New England forests and fields. These minuscule arachnids typically measure less than 3mm in length and create delicate horizontal sheet webs close to the ground among leaf litter, moss, and low vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Male Walckenaeria spiders are distinguished by their uniquely modified heads, which often feature distinctive bumps, ridges, or elevated regions that help scientists identify different species.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Walckenaeria spiders are incredibly abundant - you might walk over hundreds of their nearly invisible sheet webs during a single forest hike without ever noticing them!

children.name: Neriene
children.description: Neriene is a genus of small sheet web spiders that construct delicate, dome-shaped webs in vegetation and forest understory. These tiny spiders are known for their intricate web-building abilities, creating sheets of silk with dome or bowl-like structures that help trap flying insects. They are part of the sheet weaver spider family and are commonly found in New England's woodlands and gardens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Neriene spiders can be distinguished from other sheet weavers by their characteristic dome-shaped webs and their tendency to build webs in elevated positions among plant stems and branches. Their webs often have a more three-dimensional structure compared to the flatter sheet webs of related genera.
children.funFact: The Filmy Dome Spider's web is so delicate and transparent that it's nearly invisible to the human eye, yet strong enough to stop flying insects in mid-flight.

children.name: Pityohyphantes
children.description: Pityohyphantes is a genus of small sheet web spiders that are commonly found in forested areas throughout New England. These tiny spiders build horizontal sheet webs, often in vegetation or among leaf litter, where they wait underneath to capture small flying insects that fall onto their webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their small size (typically 2-4mm) and their characteristic horizontal sheet webs with tangled knockdown threads above. They have relatively long legs compared to their body size and are often found in cooler, shadier habitats.
children.funFact: The hammock spider gets its common name from the distinctive hammock-like shape of its horizontal sheet web, which it constructs between vegetation and uses as both a hunting platform and protective shelter.

children.name: Centromerus
children.description: Centromerus is a genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that build delicate horizontal webs close to the ground. These diminutive arachnids are typically found in leaf litter, moss, and low vegetation where they catch small flying insects in their sheet-like webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their extremely small size and the males' distinctive spurred or modified palps (reproductive structures) that give some species their common names.
children.funFact: Despite being among the smallest spiders you might encounter, Centromerus spiders are incredibly abundant - you could be walking over dozens of their tiny webs during a single forest hike without ever noticing them!

children.name: Ceratinops
children.description: Ceratinops is a genus of small, solitary bees that are part of the carpenter bee family. These bees are known for creating nests by excavating tunnels in plant stems, soft wood, or other suitable materials. They are important native pollinators that help fertilize wildflowers and other plants throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Ceratinops can be identified by their shiny, mostly hairless bodies and their habit of nesting in hollow or pithy plant stems rather than in the ground like many other small bees.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'small carpenter bees,' Ceratinops species are much gentler than their large carpenter bee cousins and rarely cause any damage to human structures, preferring to nest in natural plant materials.

children.name: Lepthyphantes
children.description: Lepthyphantes is a genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that create delicate, horizontal webs in dim, humid places. These small spiders are expert web builders, constructing fine sheet-like webs with tangled threads above them to knock flying insects down onto the catching surface below.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These spiders can be distinguished from other sheet weavers by their extremely small size and preference for indoor environments, particularly basements, cellars, and other dark, moist spaces in buildings.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'household' spiders, these tiny arachnids are actually beneficial roommates that help control populations of even smaller pests like gnats and fruit flies.

children.name: Frontinella
children.description: Frontinella is a small genus of orb weaver spiders known for their distinctive web architecture. These spiders create unique webs that combine a traditional orb web with an additional horizontal sheet web below it, giving them their common name of bowl-and-doily spiders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical orb weavers that build only vertical circular webs, Frontinella spiders construct a two-part web system with a dome-shaped orb web above and a flat sheet web below.
children.funFact: The bowl-and-doily spider's unique web design acts like a double trap - insects that bounce off the upper orb web often fall onto the lower sheet web, giving the spider a second chance to catch its prey.

children.name: Drapetisca
children.description: Drapetisca is a genus of small sheet web spiders that are specialized for life on tree bark. These spiders are part of the linyphiid family, commonly known as sheet weaver spiders, and they build horizontal sheet webs to catch small flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Drapetisca are distinguished by their flattened body shape and cryptic coloration that helps them blend perfectly with tree bark. They have distinctively long, prominent teeth on their chelicerae (mouthparts), which gives them their common name.
children.funFact: The Northern Long-toothed Sheetweaver is so well-camouflaged against tree bark that it's often overlooked even when sitting motionless in plain sight during the day.

children.name: Hypselistes
children.description: Hypselistes is a small genus of sheet web spiders that includes just one species found in New England's wetland environments. These spiders are specialized for life in boggy, peaty habitats where they build horizontal sheet webs to capture small flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hypselistes spiders can be distinguished from other sheet web weavers by their preference for acidic peatland habitats and their relatively small size with distinctive markings adapted to blend in with sphagnum moss.
children.funFact: The Peatland Sheetweb Weaver is so specialized for bog environments that it's considered an indicator species for healthy peatland ecosystems!

children.name: Linyphia
children.description: Sheetweb spiders in the genus Linyphia are small orb weavers that create distinctive horizontal sheet webs rather than the typical vertical orb webs. These spiders hang upside down beneath their flat, sheet-like webs, waiting for insects to fall onto the surface above them. They then bite through the web from below to capture their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb weavers that build vertical circular webs, Linyphia spiders construct horizontal sheet webs that look like tiny trampolines stretched between vegetation. The spider positions itself underneath the web rather than at the center or edge like most other web-building spiders.
children.funFact: The common sheetweb spider can actually 'balloon' by releasing silk threads that catch the wind, allowing them to travel through the air for miles to find new territories.

children.name: Florinda
children.description: Florinda is a small genus of sheet weaver spiders, part of the large family Linyphiidae. These tiny spiders are known for building horizontal sheet webs close to the ground, where they wait underneath to catch small flying insects that fall onto the web surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Florinda spiders can be identified by their distinctive reddish coloration and relatively robust build compared to other sheet weavers. They have a characteristic pattern of darker markings on their abdomen that helps distinguish them from similar species.
children.funFact: The Black-tailed Red Sheetweaver gets its name from both its striking reddish color and the dark markings at the tip of its abdomen, making it one of the more colorful members of the typically drab sheet weaver family.

children.name: Tapinopa
children.description: Tapinopa is a genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that are among the smallest spiders in North America. These minuscule arachnids build delicate sheet webs close to the ground and are often overlooked due to their extremely small size, typically measuring less than 2 millimeters in body length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tapinopa spiders can be distinguished from other sheet weavers by their distinctive eye arrangement and the unique structure of their reproductive organs. They have a characteristic pattern of dark lines or markings on their pale abdomen.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they could easily fit through the eye of a needle, Tapinopa spiders are skilled hunters that can capture prey items nearly as large as themselves in their sheet webs.

children.name: Tmeticus
children.description: Tmeticus is a small genus of tiny spiders belonging to the sheet weaver family (Linyphiidae), commonly known as money spiders. These diminutive arachnids are part of the vast group of spiders that construct sheet-like webs to capture their prey. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species with striking red and black coloration.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tmeticus spiders are distinguished from other money spiders by their distinctive color patterns and specific genital structures used for identification. The ornate coloration of red and black markings sets them apart from the typically more subdued colors of most other sheet weaver spiders.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'money spiders,' these tiny arachnids got their nickname from an old European belief that finding one crawling on you would bring good financial fortune!

children.name: Tusukuru
children.description: Tusukuru is a genus of tiny marine copepods, which are small crustaceans that drift in ocean waters as part of the zooplankton community. These microscopic animals are important members of marine food webs, serving as food for larger organisms while feeding on even smaller particles and organisms in the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tusukuru can be distinguished from other copepod genera by their specific body segmentation patterns and the arrangement of their swimming appendages called setae.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, copepods like Tusukuru are among the most abundant animals on Earth and play a crucial role in ocean ecosystems by helping transfer energy from tiny phytoplankton up the food chain.

children.name: Ceratinopsis
children.description: Ceratinopsis is a genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that are among the smallest spiders in North America. These minute arachnids build small sheet webs close to the ground in leaf litter, moss, and low vegetation where they hunt for even tinier prey like springtails and mites.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These spiders are distinguished by their extremely small size (often less than 2mm) and the presence of distinctive spines or projections on the male's carapace that give the genus its name, which means 'horn-face'.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, Ceratinopsis spiders are actually quite common and play an important role as predators of soil microarthropods in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Souessa
children.description: Souessa is a small genus of marine gastropod mollusks, commonly known as sea snails. These creatures are part of the diverse world of marine mollusks that inhabit coastal waters, carrying their spiral shells as they move along the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Souessa are characterized by their distinctive shell ornamentation and specific anatomical features that separate them from other marine snail genera. The single New England species, Souessa spinifera, is notable for its spiny shell projections.
children.funFact: The name 'spinifera' literally means 'spine-bearing,' referring to the characteristic spiny projections that make this sea snail's shell easily recognizable among other marine gastropods.

children.name: Tenuiphantes
children.description: Tenuiphantes is a genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders known for their delicate appearance and intricate web-building skills. These spiders are part of the linyphiid family and create horizontal sheet webs that they use to capture small flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small size, typically measuring only a few millimeters, and their distinctive striped or patterned abdomens that help distinguish them from other sheet weavers.
children.funFact: The name 'Tenuiphantes' literally means 'thin spider,' reflecting their delicate build and almost translucent appearance that can make them nearly invisible on their webs.

children.name: Bathyphantes
children.description: Bathyphantes is a genus of tiny sheet web spiders that are part of the dwarf spider family. These small arachnids are known for building delicate horizontal sheet webs close to the ground, often in leaf litter or low vegetation. They are typically pale in color and extremely small, making them easily overlooked despite being relatively common.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Bathyphantes can be distinguished from other sheet web spiders by their very pale coloration and specific genital structures that require microscopic examination to identify accurately.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that they're often smaller than a pinky fingernail, Bathyphantes spiders are skilled architects that can construct sheet webs up to several times their own body length.

children.name: Ceratinella
children.description: Ceratinella is a genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that are among the smallest spiders in North America. These minuscule arachnids build delicate horizontal sheet webs close to the ground in leaf litter and low vegetation. They are part of the large Linyphiidae family, known for their intricate web-building abilities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ceratinella spiders are distinguished by their extremely small size (often less than 2mm) and their distinctive male head modifications, which can include unusual bumps or projections used during mating displays.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that they're often overlooked, Ceratinella spiders are important predators of even smaller insects like springtails and can be quite common in forest floor ecosystems.

children.name: Origanates
children.description: Origanates is a small genus of marine flatworms found in coastal waters. These tiny, translucent creatures are part of the turbellarian flatworms, which are free-living rather than parasitic like their tapeworm relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive rostrum (snout-like projection) at the front end, which gives them their species name 'rostratus' meaning 'beaked.'
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, these flatworms are active predators that hunt even smaller marine organisms in the spaces between sand grains.

children.name: Tennesseellum
children.description: Tennesseellum is a small genus of sheet-web weaver spiders that includes just one species found in New England. These tiny spiders are part of the larger family of sheet-web weavers, which are known for building flat, sheet-like webs rather than the circular orb webs many people associate with spiders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their very small size and specific web-building behavior that creates horizontal sheet webs. They differ from other sheet-web weavers in their unique body proportions and the particular structure of their reproductive organs.
children.funFact: The Ant Sheet-web Weaver gets its common name because it's so tiny that it was once thought to mimic ants, though it's actually just a remarkably small spider that builds miniature sheet webs.

children.name: Agyneta
children.description: Agyneta is a genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that are among the smallest spiders you might encounter in New England. These diminutive arachnids are part of the large Linyphiidae family, known for building delicate horizontal sheet webs close to the ground or in low vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Agyneta spiders are distinguished by their extremely small size (usually less than 2mm) and the males' distinctive reproductive structures. They can be identified by specific features of their reproductive organs that require microscopic examination to distinguish from other tiny sheet weavers.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're often overlooked, Agyneta spiders are accomplished aerial dispersers that can 'balloon' through the air by releasing silk threads and riding air currents to colonize new habitats.

children.name: Estrandia
children.description: Estrandia is a genus of ancient marine organisms that lived hundreds of millions of years ago during the Paleozoic Era. These creatures are known only from fossil remains found in rock formations, representing some of the earliest complex life forms preserved in New England's geological record.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Estrandia fossils are characterized by their distinctive preservation patterns and unique morphological features that set them apart from other ancient marine life forms of their time period.
children.funFact: Estrandia grandaeva fossils provide a window into New England's ancient past when the region was covered by warm, shallow seas teeming with early marine life.

children.name: Gonatium
children.description: Gonatium is a small genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that are part of the large Linyphiidae family. These spiders are extremely small, typically measuring only 1-2 millimeters in length, and build delicate horizontal sheet webs close to the ground among vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gonatium spiders can be identified by their distinctively thickened palps (the small appendages near their mouth) and their characteristic web-building behavior of creating fine sheet webs in low vegetation.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, Gonatium spiders are accomplished aerialists that can 'balloon' by releasing silk threads to catch the wind and travel long distances through the air.

children.name: Grammonota
children.description: Grammonota is a genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that are among the smallest spiders in the world. These minuscule arachnids build horizontal sheet webs close to the ground and are often found in leaf litter, moss, and low vegetation where they hunt for even tinier prey like springtails and mites.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their extremely small size (often less than 2mm) and their distinctive eye arrangement, with the anterior median eyes being the largest of the eight eyes.
children.funFact: Despite being so small they could easily fit on the head of a pin, Grammonota spiders are skilled engineers that construct intricate sheet webs with knock-down threads above them to trap flying insects.

children.name: Helophora
children.description: Helophora is a small genus of moths in the cutworm family that are adapted to wetland environments. These moths are typically found in marshy areas and their caterpillars feed on various wetland plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive wing patterns and their strong association with wet, marshy habitats where their host plants grow.
children.funFact: The name Helophora literally means 'marsh bearer,' reflecting these moths' preference for wetland environments.

children.name: Hybauchenidium
children.description: Hybauchenidium is a genus of tiny marine organisms that belong to the group of creatures called foraminifera. These microscopic single-celled animals build intricate shells made of calcium carbonate and live in ocean sediments. They are part of the vast community of microorganisms that form the foundation of marine food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is characterized by its distinctive shell structure with a unique arrangement of chambers and specialized openings called apertures. The shell design of Hybauchenidium differs from other foraminifera in its specific geometric pattern and chamber organization.
children.funFact: Despite being smaller than a pinhead, foraminifera like Hybauchenidium have been used by paleontologists to determine the age of rock layers and reconstruct ancient ocean conditions from millions of years ago.

children.name: Porrhomma
children.description: Porrhomma is a genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that are found in cool, moist environments throughout the northern regions. These small spiders are part of the large Linyphiidae family and are known for building delicate sheet webs close to the ground among moss, leaf litter, and vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be recognized by their small size (typically 2-3mm) and distinctive eye arrangement, along with their preference for humid microhabitats near the forest floor.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Porrhomma spiders are important predators in forest floor ecosystems, helping control populations of even smaller invertebrates like springtails and mites.

children.name: Styloctetor
children.description: Styloctetor is a genus of very small spiders in the sheet weaver family (Linyphiidae) that are found in forest leaf litter and low vegetation. These tiny arachnids are part of the diverse group of dwarf spiders that play important roles as predators of even smaller invertebrates in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other sheet weavers by specific characteristics of their reproductive structures and the arrangement of spines on their legs, though identification typically requires microscopic examination.
children.funFact: Despite being less than 2mm in body length, these spiders are skilled hunters that help control populations of springtails, mites, and other tiny creatures in the forest floor community.

children.name: Wubana
children.description: Wubana is a small genus of ground spiders that are part of the larger family of running spiders. These are small, dark-colored spiders that live close to the ground and are active hunters rather than web-builders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wubana spiders can be distinguished from other ground spiders by their specific body proportions and the arrangement of their eyes, though detailed examination is often needed for accurate identification.
children.funFact: Despite being active hunters, Wubana spiders are so small and secretive that they often go completely unnoticed by people, living their entire lives in the leaf litter and soil surface of our forests.

children.name: Collinsia
children.description: Collinsia is a genus of small annual wildflowers in the plantain family, commonly known as blue-eyed Mary or Chinese houses. These delicate plants produce distinctive two-lipped flowers that are typically blue and white, growing in clusters along slender stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Collinsia flowers have a unique structure where the upper lip has two lobes and the lower lip has three lobes, with the middle lobe of the lower lip often folded to enclose the stamens and style.
children.funFact: The flowers of Collinsia are specially adapted for bee pollination - when a bee lands on the lower lip, its weight causes the folded middle lobe to open and deposit pollen on the bee's back.

children.name: Mermessus
children.description: Decorated-fanged Linyphiids are tiny sheet web spiders in the genus Mermessus, part of the large Linyphiidae family. These minuscule spiders are known for their intricate sheet webs and their distinctive fanged chelicerae (mouthparts). They are ground-dwelling spiders that play an important role in controlling small insect populations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Mermessus can be distinguished from other linyphiid spiders by their ornate, decorated chelicerae (fangs) and specific genital structures. They are extremely small, typically measuring less than 2-3 millimeters in body length.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Mermessus spiders are accomplished engineers, building horizontal sheet webs with knock-down threads above that cause flying insects to fall onto the sticky capture surface below.

children.name: Disembolus
children.description: Disembolus is a genus of very small, ground-dwelling spiders that are part of the sheet weaver family. These tiny arachnids are typically found in leaf litter, moss, and other debris on the forest floor where they hunt for even smaller prey like springtails and mites.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their extremely small size (usually less than 2mm) and specific genital structures that are unique to the group. They have relatively long legs compared to their body size and distinctive patterns on their abdomens.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, Disembolus spiders are active hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead stalking their tiny victims through the miniature jungle of the forest floor.

children.description: Sheetweb and Dwarf Weavers are a diverse family of small spiders that create distinctive horizontal sheet webs, often with a tangle of threads above to knock flying insects down onto the catching surface below. These tiny spiders are among the most abundant arachnids in New England, though they're often overlooked due to their small size. Many species are found in leaf litter, low vegetation, and forest floors where their delicate webs catch small prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These spiders are characterized by their small size (most under 5mm), their horizontal sheet webs with knockdown threads above, and their habit of hanging upside down beneath their webs to grab prey that falls through. Unlike orb weavers, their webs are not circular but form flat, sheet-like surfaces.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Linyphiidae is one of the largest spider families in the world, and some species are so small they can actually fly by releasing silk threads and 'ballooning' on air currents - a behavior that helps them colonize new habitats across vast distances.

children.name: Lycosidae
Pardosa
children.description: Thin-legged Wolf Spiders are a diverse group of small to medium-sized hunting spiders that don't build webs to catch their prey. Instead, they actively chase down insects and other small creatures using their excellent eyesight and quick reflexes. These spiders are common throughout New England's varied landscapes, from rocky shores to inland forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other wolf spiders, members of Pardosa have noticeably slender legs relative to their body size, giving them their 'thin-legged' name. They also tend to be smaller than their bulkier wolf spider cousins and often have more intricate patterns on their bodies.
children.funFact: Female Pardosa spiders are devoted mothers who carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets, and after the babies hatch, they climb onto mom's back for a piggyback ride until they're ready to hunt on their own.

children.name: Schizocosa
children.description: Brush-legged spiders are a group of wolf spiders known for the distinctive brushy or feathery leg ornaments found on males of many species. These medium-sized hunting spiders don't build webs to catch prey, but instead actively chase down insects on the ground. They're commonly found in leaf litter, under logs, and in grassy areas throughout New England's forests and fields.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Males are distinguished from other wolf spiders by their ornate leg decorations, including tufts of dark bristles, bands, or brush-like structures used in courtship displays. These leg ornaments are often species-specific and help females identify suitable mates.
children.funFact: Male brush-legged spiders perform elaborate courtship dances, waving their decorated legs like flags and drumming on the ground to create vibrations that attract females from distances of several inches away.

children.name: Tigrosa
children.description: Tigrosa is a genus of large, robust wolf spiders that are among the biggest spiders you'll encounter in New England. These impressive hunters are active predators that chase down their prey rather than building webs, and they're excellent mothers who carry their egg sacs and young spiderlings on their backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tigrosa spiders are distinguished from other wolf spiders by their substantial size and robust build, earning them the common name 'giant wolf spiders.' They also have distinctive eye arrangements and leg proportions that help separate them from their smaller wolf spider relatives.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating size, Tigrosa spiders are actually quite shy and will typically flee from humans, but if threatened, they can rear up on their hind legs in a defensive posture that shows off their impressive fangs.

children.name: Arctosa
children.description: Bear spiders are a genus of wolf spiders that are typically found near water sources like shorelines, streams, and wetlands. These robust hunting spiders are known for their excellent eyesight and ability to chase down prey rather than building webs to catch it. They're called 'bear spiders' because of their stocky, hairy appearance that resembles tiny bears.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bear spiders can be distinguished from other wolf spiders by their preference for aquatic or semi-aquatic habitats and their typically darker, more mottled coloration that helps them blend in with sandy or rocky shoreline environments.
children.funFact: Some bear spider species can actually walk on water and will dive beneath the surface when threatened, carrying an air bubble with them to breathe underwater.

children.name: Hogna
children.description: Hogna wolf spiders are among the largest and most impressive spiders found in New England. These robust hunters have excellent eyesight and actively chase down their prey rather than building webs to catch it. They're ground-dwelling spiders that can often be seen running across forest floors, meadows, and even into homes during cooler months.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hogna spiders are distinguished from other wolf spiders by their large size and robust build, with some species reaching over an inch in body length. They have particularly prominent front-facing eyes that give them keen vision for hunting.
children.funFact: Female Hogna wolf spiders are devoted mothers who carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets, and after the babies hatch, they ride on their mother's back for protection until their first molt.

children.name: Trochosa
children.description: Trochosa is a genus of wolf spiders that are well-adapted to life on the ground in various habitats throughout New England. These medium-sized spiders are excellent hunters that actively chase down their prey rather than building webs to catch food. Like other wolf spiders, females carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets and later carry their newly hatched spiderlings on their backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Trochosa wolf spiders can be distinguished from other wolf spider genera by their robust build and distinctive eye arrangement, along with specific patterns on their carapace and abdomen that vary by species.
children.funFact: Trochosa spiders are capable swimmers and some species can actually run across the surface of water when escaping predators or pursuing prey.

children.name: Gladicosa
children.description: Sword Wolf Spiders are a genus of ground-dwelling hunting spiders that actively chase down their prey rather than building webs. These medium-sized spiders are known for their excellent eyesight and swift movements as they patrol forest floors and woodland edges throughout New England.
