children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other wolf spiders, Gladicosa species have distinctive markings and body proportions that help identify them, along with specific behavioral patterns during mating season.
children.funFact: The Drumming Sword Wolf Spider gets its name from the male's courtship behavior - he drums rhythmically on the ground and waves his legs to attract females, creating vibrations that can be felt through the substrate.

children.name: Rabidosa
children.description: Rabidosa is a genus of large, robust wolf spiders that are among the most impressive arachnids you'll encounter in New England. These spiders are excellent hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, but instead actively chase down their meals with remarkable speed and agility. They're particularly associated with wetland areas and can often be found near ponds, streams, and marshy habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rabidosa wolf spiders are distinguished from other wolf spider genera by their large size, distinctive eye arrangement, and their strong association with aquatic environments. They have particularly robust front legs and a characteristic pattern of stripes or spots that helps separate them from similar-looking wolf spiders.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating name, Rabidosa spiders got their scientific name from the Latin word 'rabidus' meaning 'raging' or 'fierce,' referring to their aggressive hunting style rather than any connection to the disease rabies.

children.name: Pirata
children.description: Pirate wolf spiders are semi-aquatic hunting spiders that live near water sources like ponds, streams, and wetlands. These medium-sized spiders are active hunters that chase down their prey rather than building webs to catch it. They get their common name from their bold, predatory behavior and their habit of 'pirating' territory near water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most wolf spiders that live in dry habitats, pirate wolf spiders are closely associated with aquatic environments and can actually run across the water's surface. They have longer legs relative to their body size compared to typical ground-dwelling wolf spiders.
children.funFact: Pirate wolf spiders can dive underwater to escape predators and will stay submerged for several minutes, breathing air trapped in the fine hairs on their bodies.

children.name: Geolycosa
children.description: Burrowing wolf spiders are specialized hunters that create underground homes by digging vertical burrows in sandy or loose soil. Unlike most wolf spiders that wander freely, these species spend much of their time in their burrows, emerging to hunt or mate. They line their burrows with silk and often create a distinctive collar or turret around the entrance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These wolf spiders are set apart by their burrowing lifestyle and the permanent silk-lined tunnels they create, rather than wandering on the surface like most of their relatives. Their burrow entrances are often marked by distinctive silk collars or small turrets made of soil and debris.
children.funFact: Female burrowing wolf spiders carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets and later allow hundreds of tiny spiderlings to ride on their backs - all while living in their underground burrows!

children.name: Alopecosa
children.description: Fox Spiders are a genus of wolf spiders known for their robust build and hunting prowess. These ground-dwelling predators don't build webs to catch prey, but instead actively hunt insects and other small creatures using their excellent eyesight and speed. Like other wolf spiders, female Fox Spiders are devoted mothers who carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets and later carry their newly hatched spiderlings on their backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fox Spiders can be distinguished from other wolf spider genera by their relatively stocky bodies and specific arrangements of spines on their legs. They tend to be medium-sized wolf spiders with distinctive eye patterns and leg proportions that help experts identify them in the field.
children.funFact: The name 'Alopecosa' literally means 'fox-like' in Greek, referring to these spiders' cunning hunting behavior and their tendency to be most active during twilight hours when they stalk their prey like miniature foxes.

children.name: Piratula
children.description: Piratula is a genus of small wolf spiders that are excellent hunters, actively pursuing their prey rather than building webs to catch it. These spiders have keen eyesight and strong legs that make them swift runners across various terrains. Like other wolf spiders, female Piratula carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets and later carry their newly hatched spiderlings on their backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Piratula spiders are distinguished from other wolf spider genera by their smaller size and specific eye arrangement patterns. They typically have a more compact body structure compared to larger wolf spider relatives.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Piratula' means 'little pirate,' which perfectly captures these tiny predators' bold hunting behavior as they fearlessly chase down prey much like their seafaring namesakes!

children.name: Allocosa
children.description: Allocosa is a genus of wolf spiders that are medium-sized, ground-dwelling hunters found in various habitats across North America. These spiders are active predators that chase down their prey rather than building webs, and like other wolf spiders, the females carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets and later carry their young on their backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Allocosa wolf spiders can be distinguished from other wolf spider genera by specific patterns in their eye arrangement and unique markings on their carapace and abdomen. They typically have a more robust build compared to some of their wolf spider relatives.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Allocosa funerea, gets its species name from the Latin word meaning 'funeral' or 'dark,' likely referring to its somber coloration.

children.name: Trabeops
children.description: Trabeops is a small genus of orb weaver spiders found in North America. These spiders are part of the larger family of orb weavers that build the classic circular webs we often see in gardens and forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Trabeops spiders can be distinguished from other orb weavers by their distinctive eye arrangement and specific patterns on their abdomen, along with unique structural features in their web-building organs.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Trabeops aurantiacus, gets its species name from the Latin word for 'golden' or 'orange-colored,' referring to its beautiful coloration.

children.name: Trebacosa
children.description: Trebacosa is a genus of wolf spiders that are semi-aquatic, meaning they live near water and can actually run across the water's surface when hunting or escaping danger. These spiders are active hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead relying on their excellent eyesight and speed to chase down insects and other small creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most wolf spiders that live on dry land, Trebacosa spiders are specially adapted for life around water with water-repellent hairs that help them stay afloat and move across the surface.
children.funFact: The Marx pirate spider gets its common name from its habit of 'pirating' prey from the water surface, snatching up insects that have fallen in or are trying to drink.

children.name: Varacosa
children.description: Varacosa is a genus of wolf spiders that are active hunters, using their excellent eyesight to stalk and chase down prey rather than building webs. These medium-sized spiders are typically brown or gray with subtle patterns that help them blend into their surroundings. Like other wolf spiders, females carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets and later carry their newly hatched spiderlings on their backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Varacosa spiders can be distinguished from other wolf spider genera by their specific eye arrangement and leg proportions, though identification often requires close examination of anatomical details. They tend to be more robust in build compared to some of their wolf spider relatives.
children.funFact: Female Varacosa spiders are devoted mothers - if their egg sac is removed, they will frantically search for it and can even be tricked into accepting a small ball of cotton as a replacement!

children.description: Wolf spiders are active hunting spiders that don't build webs to catch prey. Instead, they rely on their excellent eyesight and speed to chase down insects and other small creatures. These robust spiders are found in a wide variety of habitats from forests to fields to shorelines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wolf spiders have two large eyes in the front row and distinctive eye arrangements that give them superior vision compared to most spiders. Many species carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets and later carry their spiderlings on their backs.
children.funFact: Female wolf spiders are devoted mothers - after their eggs hatch, the tiny spiderlings climb onto their mother's back and ride around for about a week until they're ready to hunt on their own.

children.name: Theridiidae
Steatoda
children.description: False widow spiders are medium-sized web-building spiders that are close relatives of the famous black widow spiders. They create irregular, tangled webs in corners, crevices, and sheltered spots around buildings, gardens, and natural areas. These spiders are generally brown or dark-colored with various markings, and they're commonly found throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true black widow spiders, false widows lack the distinctive red hourglass marking and have less potent venom. They can be identified by their bulbous abdomens with pale markings or stripes, and their habit of building messy cobwebs rather than the organized orb webs of many other spiders.
children.funFact: The name 'combfoot' comes from the row of curved bristles on their hind legs that they use like a comb to throw silk over prey caught in their webs.

children.name: Theridion
children.description: Theridion is a genus of small cobweb spiders that build irregular, tangled webs to catch their prey. These spiders are typically found in gardens, forests, and around human structures, where they construct their messy-looking webs in corners, between branches, or along fences and walls.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Theridion spiders can be distinguished from other cobweb spiders by their relatively long legs and small, rounded abdomens. Many species in this genus have distinctive color patterns and are smaller than their more famous cousin, the black widow.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, Theridion spiders are accomplished architects that can rebuild their entire web in just a few hours if it gets damaged.

children.name: Enoplognatha
children.description: Enoplognatha is a genus of small cobweb spiders that are commonly found throughout New England's gardens, meadows, and woodland edges. These delicate spiders are known for building irregular, tangled webs among vegetation where they catch small flying insects. Most species in this genus are quite small, typically measuring less than 6mm in body length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Enoplognatha spiders can be identified by their relatively large, bulbous abdomens compared to their small cephalothorax (front body section), and their habit of building loose, irregular cobwebs rather than the organized orb webs of many other spider families.
children.funFact: The common candy-striped spider gets its name from the distinctive red stripes that run along its pale abdomen, making it look like it's wearing a tiny striped sweater!

children.name: Latrodectus
children.description: Widow spiders are medium-sized spiders known for their potent venom and the females' tendency to sometimes eat males after mating, which gives them their common name. All widow spiders have round abdomens and relatively long, thin legs, and they build irregular, sticky webs in sheltered locations. The females are significantly larger than males and are the ones typically encountered by humans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Widow spiders can be identified by their distinctive hourglass-shaped marking on the underside of their round abdomen, though the color varies by species. They have a comb-like structure on their hind legs that helps them wrap prey in silk.
children.funFact: Despite their fearsome reputation, widow spider bites are rarely fatal to humans - only the female's bite is medically significant, and they are actually quite shy spiders that prefer to flee rather than bite when disturbed.

children.name: Parasteatoda
children.description: The Colourful Comb-footed Spiders are a genus of small to medium-sized spiders known for their intricate cobwebs and distinctive body patterns. These spiders have a globular abdomen and are part of the larger comb-footed spider family, getting their name from the special serrated bristles on their hind legs used to throw silk over prey. They're commonly found around human dwellings where they build irregular, three-dimensional webs in corners and sheltered spaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other comb-footed spiders, Parasteatoda species typically display more vibrant coloration and distinct markings on their abdomens. They also tend to be more tolerant of disturbance and often rebuild their webs in the same location repeatedly.
children.funFact: The Common House Spider can produce up to seven different types of silk from different glands, each with unique properties for specific web-building and prey-capture functions.

children.name: Robertus
children.description: Robertus is a genus of small, dark-colored spiders that belong to the theridiid family, commonly known as cobweb weavers. These tiny spiders are typically found in leaf litter, under logs, and in other moist ground-level habitats throughout New England. They build irregular, three-dimensional webs close to the ground where they capture small insects and other tiny prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Robertus spiders are distinguished from other cobweb weavers by their very small size (usually less than 3mm), dark coloration, and preference for ground-level microhabitats rather than the elevated web locations favored by many of their relatives.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Robertus spiders are excellent indicators of healthy forest ecosystems, as they require stable moisture levels and undisturbed leaf litter to thrive.

children.name: Crustulina
children.description: Crustulina is a small genus of tiny cobweb weavers that build delicate, irregular webs in sheltered spots like leaf litter, under bark, and in forest debris. These diminutive spiders are part of the large cobweb weaver family and are skilled at catching small flying insects in their sticky traps. They're often overlooked due to their small size and secretive nature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Crustulina are distinguished by their very small size (typically less than 3mm) and their habit of building webs in cryptic microhabitats rather than open spaces. They have relatively long legs compared to their compact bodies, helping them navigate their tangled webs.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that they could easily fit on your fingernail, Crustulina spiders are important predators of even smaller insects like gnats and midges, helping control populations of these sometimes pesky creatures.

children.name: Asagena
children.description: Asagena is a small genus of cobweb spiders that build irregular, tangled webs to catch their prey. These tiny spiders are part of the larger cobweb weaver family and are known for their distinctive markings and web-building behavior.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Asagena can be identified by their characteristic spotted patterns and relatively small size compared to other cobweb weavers. They construct less organized, more irregular webs than their close relatives.
children.funFact: The Two-spotted Cobweb Spider is so small that its entire body could fit on the head of a pin, yet it's capable of catching prey much larger than itself in its sticky web.

children.name: Yunohamella
children.description: Yunohamella is a small genus of orb weaver spiders known for their intricate web-building abilities and distinctive body patterns. These spiders are part of the larger orb weaver family and are characterized by their compact size and specialized web construction techniques.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Yunohamella can be distinguished from other orb weavers by their unique abdominal markings and the specific geometric patterns they weave into their webs.
children.funFact: The genus name Yunohamella reflects the delicate, almost musical quality of their web vibrations, which they use to detect prey and communicate.

children.name: Neospintharus
children.description: Neospintharus is a small genus of tiny orb weaver spiders that have adopted a parasitic lifestyle. These minute spiders live on the webs of much larger orb weavers, stealing food and sometimes even feeding on their host's eggs or young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical orb weavers that build their own webs, Neospintharus spiders are kleptoparasites that live as uninvited guests on other spiders' webs. They are extremely small, usually less than 2mm in length, making them much tinier than their hosts.
children.funFact: The Horned Parasitic Cobweaver gets its name from small horn-like projections on its abdomen, and despite being a freeloader, it's so small that host spiders often don't even notice its presence on their webs.

children.name: Euryopis
children.description: Ant-eating spiders are tiny specialized hunters that have evolved to prey almost exclusively on ants. These small cobweb spiders are part of the larger cobweaver family but have developed unique hunting strategies to tackle their well-defended ant prey. They build modified webs and use special techniques to overcome ants' strong jaws and chemical defenses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cobweavers that catch flying insects in their webs, Euryopis spiders specifically target ants crawling on surfaces. They have proportionally longer legs and modified web structures compared to their relatives, helping them safely capture and handle their aggressive prey.
children.funFact: These spiders can take down ants much larger than themselves by quickly wrapping them in silk and injecting venom before the ant can use its powerful mandibles to fight back.

children.name: Theridula
children.description: Theridula is a genus of very small cobweb spiders that build tiny, irregular webs in vegetation and leaf litter. These minute spiders are part of the larger cobweb weaver family and are known for their delicate construction skills despite their tiny size.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Theridula spiders are distinguished by their extremely small size and the presence of two small bumps or tubercles on their abdomen, which gives them their common name 'bitubercled cobweavers.'
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, Theridula spiders are actually quite common in forest floor habitats where they help control populations of even tinier insects like springtails and fungus gnats.

children.name: Spintharus
children.description: Spintharus is a genus of tiny orb weaver spiders known for their distinctive triangular abdomens and intricate web-building behavior. These small spiders are part of the orb weaver family and create delicate, circular webs to catch their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their uniquely shaped triangular or cone-like abdomens that come to a point, making them easily distinguishable from other orb weavers with rounded abdomens.
children.funFact: Despite being orb weavers, some Spintharus species are known to abandon their webs and become wandering hunters, which is unusual behavior for this typically web-dependent spider family.

children.name: Wamba
children.description: Wamba is a small genus of marine gastropod mollusks, commonly known as sea snails. These creatures are characterized by their spiral shells and soft bodies that they can retract into their protective shells when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wamba species are distinguished by their distinctive shell morphology and specific anatomical features that separate them from other marine gastropod genera.
children.funFact: Like many sea snails, Wamba species use a specialized feeding structure called a radula - essentially a ribbon-like tongue covered in tiny teeth - to scrape food from surfaces.

children.name: Thymoites
children.description: Thymoites is a small genus of orb weaver spiders that includes just a handful of species worldwide. These spiders are part of the large orb weaver family and construct circular webs to catch flying insects. In New England, we have only one representative of this genus - the Spotted Cobweaver.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Thymoites spiders can be recognized by their relatively small size and distinctive web construction patterns that differ from typical orb weavers. They tend to build their webs in more sheltered locations compared to many of their orb weaver relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'cobweavers,' these spiders actually build orb webs rather than the irregular cobweb-style webs that most people associate with the term 'cobweb.'

children.name: Phoroncidia
children.description: Mushroom Comb-footed Spiders are tiny orb weavers that get their name from their unusual body shape, which resembles a small mushroom when viewed from the side. These spiders are among the smallest orb weavers in North America, with females reaching only about 2-3 millimeters in length. They build small, delicate webs in low vegetation and leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb weavers, Phoroncidia spiders have a distinctive mushroom-shaped abdomen that overhangs their cephalothorax (head region). Their webs are also much smaller and less organized than the classic circular orb webs of their larger relatives.
children.funFact: These tiny spiders are so small that their entire web can fit on a single leaf, and they're often overlooked because they're active mainly at night and hide during the day.

children.name: Dipoena
children.description: Dipoena is a genus of small orb weaver spiders that build distinctive webs with reduced or missing spiral threads. These tiny spiders are often found in low vegetation where they construct their modified orb webs to catch small flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical orb weavers, Dipoena spiders create webs with very few or no sticky spiral threads, instead relying primarily on the radial framework to capture prey.
children.funFact: Despite being orb weavers, some Dipoena species have evolved to be kleptoparasites, stealing prey from the webs of larger spiders rather than relying solely on their own reduced webs.

children.name: Cryptachaea
children.description: Cryptachaea is a genus of small comb-footed spiders that are part of the cobweb weaver family. These tiny spiders build irregular, tangled webs and are known for their secretive nature, often hiding in cracks and crevices during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Cryptachaea can be distinguished from other cobweb weavers by their small size and specific genital structures that require microscopic examination for proper identification.
children.funFact: The name 'Cryptachaea' literally means 'hidden Achaea,' reflecting these spiders' secretive lifestyle and their close relationship to the more well-known house spider genus Achaea.

children.name: Rhomphaea
children.description: Stretched Thief Spiders are tiny orb weavers with elongated, stretched-out bodies that give them their distinctive name. These small spiders are known for their peculiar habit of invading other spiders' webs to steal prey, rather than building substantial webs of their own.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical orb weavers, these spiders have extremely elongated abdomens that can be several times longer than they are wide. They also lack the robust web-building behavior of their relatives, instead preferring to live as kleptoparasites in other spiders' webs.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'thief spiders,' they don't just steal food - they sometimes eat the host spider too, making them both burglars and predators in the spider world.

children.name: Argyrodes
children.description: Dewdrop spiders are tiny, silvery spiders that get their name from their shimmering, metallic appearance that resembles morning dewdrops. These small arachnids are kleptoparasites, meaning they live in or near the webs of larger spiders and steal their prey rather than building their own hunting webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dewdrop spiders can be identified by their distinctive silver or metallic coloration and their extremely small size, typically measuring only 1-4mm in length. Unlike most spiders, they don't build webs for catching prey but instead pilfer food from other spiders' webs.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny thieves, dewdrop spiders are so small and stealthy that their host spiders often don't even notice them stealing food from their webs.

children.name: Platnickina
children.description: Platnick's Cobweb Spiders are small, delicate spiders that belong to the cobweb weaver family. They build irregular, tangled webs to catch their prey, similar to their more famous house spider relatives. These spiders are quite rare and were only recently recognized as their own distinct group.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These spiders can be distinguished from other cobweb weavers by their unique body proportions and the specific patterns on their abdomen. They are also notably smaller than most other members of the cobweb weaver family.
children.funFact: This genus was named after Norman Platnick, a renowned spider expert who described over 1,800 spider species during his career - more than any other arachnologist in history.

children.name: Hentziectypus
children.description: Hentziectypus is a small genus of orb weaver spiders that build circular, sticky webs to catch flying insects. These spiders are part of the larger orb weaver family and are known for their intricate web-spinning abilities. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species, the Fingered Cobweaver.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive fingered or lobed projections on their bodies, which give the Fingered Cobweaver its common name. They also have a more globular or rounded abdomen compared to many other orb weavers.
children.funFact: Despite being called a 'cobweaver,' the Fingered Cobweaver actually builds organized orb webs rather than the messy cobwebs typically associated with house spiders.

children.name: Episinus
children.description: Square-ended Cobweb Spiders are tiny orb weavers that create distinctive webs with a unique geometric pattern. These small spiders build webs that have a characteristic square or rectangular frame, quite different from the typical circular orb webs most people are familiar with. They are part of the larger cobweb weaver family but have evolved this specialized web architecture.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical orb weavers that build circular webs, these spiders construct webs with distinct square or rectangular outer frames. Their webs also tend to be much smaller and more compact than those of their circular-web-building relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'cobweb spiders,' their geometric webs are actually quite organized and purposeful - the square frame helps them maximize catching efficiency in tight spaces like between plant stems.

children.description: Comb-footed spiders are small to medium-sized web builders named for the distinctive row of curved bristles (like a comb) on their hind legs, which they use to throw silk over their prey. Most species build irregular, three-dimensional cobwebs rather than the classic orb webs, creating tangled-looking webs in corners, under eaves, and in vegetation. This diverse family includes both harmless house spiders and the potentially dangerous widow spiders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The comb of serrated bristles on their fourth pair of legs is unique among spiders and serves as their primary identifying feature. Their webs are typically irregular and three-dimensional, lacking the organized spiral pattern of orb weavers.
children.funFact: Some comb-footed spiders, like the dewdrop spiders, are kleptoparasites that steal food from other spiders' webs rather than catching their own prey.

children.name: Thomisidae
Xysticus
children.description: Ground crab spiders are a diverse group of small to medium-sized hunting spiders that get their name from their crab-like appearance and ground-dwelling habits. These spiders have flattened bodies with front legs that are typically longer and held out to the sides, giving them their characteristic sideways scuttling movement. Unlike web-building spiders, they are active hunters that ambush prey from hiding spots on the ground, under rocks, or among leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ground crab spiders can be distinguished from other crab spiders by their preference for ground habitats rather than flowers or vegetation, and their generally more muted brown, gray, or tan coloration that helps them blend with soil and debris.
children.funFact: Some ground crab spiders can change their body color slightly over several days to better match their surroundings, making them nearly invisible to both prey and predators.

children.name: Mecaphesa
children.description: Mecaphesa is a genus of small crab spiders known for their ability to change color to match flowers and other surfaces where they hunt. These ambush predators sit motionless on petals and leaves, waiting to grab unsuspecting insects that come to feed. Like other crab spiders, they hold their front legs out sideways and can walk forwards, backwards, and sideways with equal ease.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mecaphesa spiders are distinguished from other crab spider genera by their relatively robust build and specific arrangements of spines and setae on their legs. They also have distinctive eye arrangements and genital structures that separate them from closely related flower crab spiders.
children.funFact: These spiders can actually change from white to yellow and back again over several days by moving pigment granules in their cells, allowing them to perfectly match different colored flowers as they hunt.

children.name: Ozyptila
children.description: Leaflitter Crab Spiders are small hunting spiders that live among fallen leaves and low vegetation on the forest floor. These tiny predators are part of the crab spider family, named for their ability to move sideways and backwards like crabs. They don't build webs but instead actively hunt small insects and other prey in the leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crab spiders that often sit on flowers waiting for pollinators, Ozyptila species are ground-dwellers with darker, more camouflaged coloring that helps them blend into the brown and mottled leaf litter where they hunt.
children.funFact: These spiders are so small and well-camouflaged that they're often overlooked by naturalists, but they play an important role as predators of tiny insects like springtails and midges in forest floor ecosystems.

children.name: Bassaniana
children.description: Bassaniana is a genus of crab spiders that are masters of camouflage, typically found on tree bark and wooden surfaces. These small spiders hold their front legs out sideways like crabs and can move sideways and backwards with ease. They are ambush predators that wait motionless for unsuspecting insects to come within striking distance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crab spiders that prefer flowers, Bassaniana species specialize in living on bark and wooden surfaces where their mottled coloration provides excellent camouflage. They tend to be flatter than other crab spiders, helping them blend seamlessly against tree trunks.
children.funFact: The Multicolored Bark Crab Spider can actually change its coloration over several days to better match the bark it's sitting on, shifting between gray, brown, and white patterns.

children.name: Misumena
children.description: Flower crab spiders are small hunting spiders that don't build webs but instead wait motionless on flowers to ambush visiting insects. They get their name from their crab-like appearance and ability to walk sideways and backwards. These patient predators are masters of camouflage, often matching the color of the flowers they hunt on.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crab spiders, flower crab spiders can actually change their body color from white to yellow and back again to match different flowers. They also have distinctively long front legs that they hold outstretched like a crab's claws.
children.funFact: The Goldenrod Crab Spider can change from white to bright yellow in just a few days by moving pigments in their skin cells, making them nearly invisible to both prey and predators on flowers like daisies and goldenrod.

children.name: Misumessus
children.description: Misumessus is a genus of crab spiders known for their ability to change color and their ambush hunting style. These spiders don't build webs to catch prey, but instead sit motionless on flowers and plants, waiting to grab unsuspecting insects that come within reach. They get their name from their crab-like appearance and sideways movement.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crab spiders, Misumessus species have a distinctly elongated, oval-shaped abdomen rather than a rounded one. Their front two pairs of legs are noticeably longer and more robust than the back pairs, giving them excellent grasping ability.
children.funFact: The American Green Crab Spider can slowly change its color from white to yellow to green over several days to perfectly match the flower it's hunting on, making it nearly invisible to both prey and predators.

children.name: Misumenoides
children.description: Misumenoides is a genus of crab spiders known for their excellent camouflage abilities and ambush hunting style. These spiders get their name from their crab-like appearance and movement, with front legs that extend sideways and the ability to walk forwards, backwards, and sideways with equal ease.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their ability to change color over several days to match the flowers they hunt on, and their characteristic white or light-colored bands across their bodies.
children.funFact: White-banded crab spiders can change from white to yellow and back again to perfectly match the flowers they're hunting on, making them nearly invisible to unsuspecting pollinator prey.

children.name: Tmarus
children.description: Octopus spiders are a genus of crab spiders known for their distinctive angular, tuberculated (bumpy) appearance that helps them blend in perfectly with tree bark and lichen. These small hunters don't build webs but instead wait motionlessly on tree trunks to ambush passing prey. Like other crab spiders, they can move sideways and have front legs that are longer and more robust than their back legs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other crab spiders that are found on flowers, Tmarus species are specialized bark-dwellers with pronounced angular bumps and projections on their bodies that create excellent camouflage against rough tree surfaces.
children.funFact: The name 'octopus spider' comes from their habit of spreading their eight legs in different directions while pressed against tree bark, creating a distinctive silhouette that resembles a tiny octopus.

children.description: Crab spiders are named for their crab-like appearance and sideways scuttling movement, with their front two pairs of legs held wide and often longer than their back legs. These are sit-and-wait predators that don't build webs to catch prey, instead ambushing insects that come within reach. They're masters of camouflage, often matching the color of flowers, bark, or leaves where they hunt.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike web-building spiders, crab spiders have robust front legs adapted for grabbing prey and can walk sideways and backwards as easily as forwards. Their flattened bodies and ability to hold their legs out horizontally give them their distinctive crab-like posture.
children.funFact: Some flower crab spiders can actually change color over several days to match the bloom they're hunting on, shifting between white and yellow to blend perfectly with their floral hunting grounds.

children.name: Gnaphosidae
Sergiolus
children.description: Sergiolus spiders are small ground-dwelling hunters that patrol the forest floor and leaf litter in search of tiny prey. These compact spiders are known for their intricate patterns and markings, which often include spots, stripes, or other distinctive designs that help them blend into their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their small size, typically under 5mm, and their characteristic body patterns that often include eye-catching spots or geometric designs. They have relatively robust bodies compared to other ground spiders and distinctive eye arrangements.
children.funFact: Some Sergiolus species are skilled ant mimics, copying the appearance and movements of ants to avoid predators and get close to their prey undetected.

children.name: Zelotes
children.description: Zelotes is a genus of ground spiders that are commonly found scurrying across the forest floor and hiding under rocks, logs, and leaf litter. These small, dark-colored spiders are active hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead relying on their speed and agility to chase down insects and other small arthropods. They're most active at night when they emerge from their daytime hiding spots to hunt.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Zelotes spiders can be identified by their flattened bodies, dark coloration (usually black or dark brown), and relatively long legs that help them move quickly across the ground. Unlike web-building spiders, they have less developed spinnerets and produce silk mainly for creating egg sacs and lining their retreats.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, Zelotes spiders are fierce predators that can take down prey much larger than themselves, including other spiders!

children.name: Drassyllus
children.description: Drassyllus is a genus of small ground spiders that are active hunters, prowling for prey rather than building webs to catch their meals. These compact spiders are typically found under rocks, logs, or leaf litter during the day, emerging at night to hunt for small insects and other tiny arthropods. They're part of the ground spider family and are common but often overlooked residents of New England's forests and gardens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Drassyllus spiders can be identified by their relatively flattened bodies and their habit of living close to the ground under cover objects. Unlike web-building spiders, they have strong legs adapted for running and hunting rather than silk production for prey capture.
children.funFact: These spiders are sometimes called "mousehole spiders" because they often retreat into small, silk-lined chambers they create under stones or in crevices, similar to how a mouse might hide in a tiny burrow.

children.name: Micaria
children.description: Micaria spiders are small ground spiders that hunt actively on the forest floor and other surfaces. These tiny predators are known for their ant-like appearance and behavior, often moving in quick, jerky motions that help them blend in with their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Micaria spiders can be identified by their shiny, often metallic-looking bodies and their distinctive habit of raising their front legs while walking, making them look remarkably similar to ants.
children.funFact: These spiders are such convincing ant mimics that they can often be found running alongside real ants without being detected, giving them protection from predators and better access to prey.

children.name: Herpyllus
children.description: Herpyllus is a genus of ground spiders known for their distinctive markings and nocturnal hunting behavior. These spiders are medium-sized hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead actively stalking insects and other small arthropods on the ground and on surfaces like tree bark and building walls.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their robust build, distinctive abdominal patterns, and strong legs adapted for running rather than web-building. They have eight eyes arranged in two rows and powerful chelicerae (mouthparts) for subduing prey.
children.funFact: The Eastern Parson Spider gets its common name from the white marking on its abdomen that resembles the white collar or cravat traditionally worn by parsons and clergy members.

children.name: Cesonia
children.description: Cesonia is a small genus of ground-dwelling spiders known for their secretive hunting behavior. These spiders are active predators that hunt on the ground surface and under debris, using stealth rather than webs to catch their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Cesonia can be identified by their distinctive body markings and their preference for hunting along the ground rather than building webs like many other spider groups.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'stealthy' ground spiders, Cesonia spiders are actually quite fast runners when they need to chase down prey or escape from predators.

children.name: Callilepis
children.description: Callilepis is a genus of ground spiders that are active hunters, preferring to chase down their prey rather than build webs. These small, fast-moving spiders are typically found under rocks, logs, or leaf litter where they hunt for other small arthropods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Callilepis can be recognized by their relatively flattened bodies and distinctive eye arrangement, with the front row of eyes being much smaller than the back row.
children.funFact: The name Callilepis means 'beautiful scale' in Greek, referring to the distinctive scale-like patterns often found on their abdomens.

children.name: Gnaphosa
children.description: Gnaphosa is a genus of ground spiders that are active hunters, preferring to chase down their prey rather than build webs to catch it. These spiders are typically dark-colored and medium-sized, with robust bodies built for life on the ground. They are nocturnal hunters that spend their days hiding under rocks, logs, or leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gnaphosa spiders can be identified by their flattened, elongated bodies and relatively long legs that are well-suited for running across various surfaces. They have distinctive spinning organs called spinnerets that they use to create silken retreats rather than hunting webs.
children.funFact: Despite not building webs to catch prey, Gnaphosa spiders are skilled silk producers that create tube-like retreats under stones or bark where they rest during the day and molt safely.

children.name: Haplodrassus
children.description: Haplodrassus is a genus of ground spiders that are small, typically brown or gray hunters that actively search for prey rather than building webs. These spiders are nocturnal predators that spend their days hiding under stones, logs, or in leaf litter, emerging at night to hunt for small insects and other tiny invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Haplodrassus can be distinguished from other ground spiders by their relatively flattened body shape and distinctive arrangement of eyes in two rows. They also have a characteristic pattern of spines on their legs that helps with identification.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'ground spiders,' Haplodrassus species do produce silk - they use it to create protective retreats and egg sacs rather than prey-catching webs.

children.description: Stealthy Ground Spiders are nocturnal hunters that prowl along the ground and under rocks, logs, and leaf litter in search of prey. These compact, dark-colored spiders are built for stealth, with flattened bodies that help them slip into tight crevices and hide during the day. They don't build webs to catch food, instead relying on their speed and hunting skills to capture insects and other small arthropods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike web-building spiders, ground spiders are active hunters with relatively long, sturdy legs adapted for running. They typically have dark, muted coloration and tough, leathery-looking abdomens that help them blend into their ground-level habitat.
children.funFact: Many ground spiders line their hiding spots with silk to create cozy retreats, and some species can run backwards almost as quickly as they move forward to escape danger.

children.name: Tetragnathidae
Tetragnatha
children.description: Stretch spiders are aptly named for their remarkably elongated, slender bodies and extremely long legs that they often stretch out in a straight line along plant stems or water edges. These orb weavers build horizontal or slightly inclined webs, typically near water sources like ponds, streams, and wetlands. When threatened, they press their bodies against vegetation and extend their legs forward and backward, making them nearly invisible as they mimic twigs or grass blades.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb weavers, stretch spiders have disproportionately long, thin bodies and legs, and they hold their legs in a characteristic straight-line position when at rest. Their webs are also distinctively horizontal rather than vertical, and they often have a small retreat area connected to the main web.
children.funFact: When courting, male stretch spiders must carefully approach females by plucking specific patterns on the web threads - one wrong vibration could result in the male becoming the female's next meal instead of her mate!

children.name: Pachygnatha
children.description: Thickjawed orbweavers are small spiders with unusually large, prominent jaws (chelicerae) that give them their common name. Despite being related to typical orbweavers, these spiders don't build the classic circular webs we usually associate with that family. Instead, they live closer to the ground in vegetation and leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their oversized jaws are the most obvious feature that sets them apart from other orbweavers. They also have a more elongated body shape and tend to be found in ground-level habitats rather than building aerial webs.
children.funFact: These spiders have essentially abandoned web-building and become active hunters, using their powerful jaws to capture prey directly rather than waiting for insects to fly into a web.

children.name: Leucauge
children.description: Orchard spiders are beautiful orb weavers known for their stunning metallic colors and delicate webs. These medium-sized spiders typically display silvery, golden, or greenish hues that shimmer in sunlight, making them some of the most visually striking spiders in New England. They build circular webs in gardens, orchards, and woodland edges where they catch flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical orb weavers that hide during the day, orchard spiders often sit prominently in the center of their webs, displaying their brilliant metallic coloration. Their webs are also notably more horizontal than the vertical webs of most other orb weavers.
children.funFact: Orchard spiders get their metallic shine from special light-reflecting cells called guanocytes that contain crystalline deposits, essentially making them living jewels of the spider world.

children.name: Meta
children.description: Cave Orbweavers are specialized spiders that build their webs in caves, under overhangs, and other dark, sheltered places. These spiders have adapted to low-light environments and create orb-shaped webs to catch flying insects that venture into their dim habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most orb weavers that build webs in open areas, Cave Orbweavers specifically seek out dark, protected spaces like cave entrances and deep rock crevices. They have longer legs relative to their body size compared to many other orb weavers.
children.funFact: Cave Orbweavers often leave a sector of their web open, creating an incomplete orb with a gap that may help them detect prey vibrations more effectively in the echoing environment of caves.

children.name: Glenognatha
children.description: Glenognatha is a genus of very small orb weaver spiders known for their elongated jaws and diminutive size. These tiny spiders build small, delicate orb webs to catch even tinier prey like gnats and midges. Despite their small stature, they are skilled web architects that construct perfectly symmetrical circular webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Glenognatha spiders are distinguished from other orb weavers by their extremely small size (often less than 3mm) and notably elongated chelicerae (jaws). Their webs are also much smaller and more delicate than those of typical orb weavers.
children.funFact: The Dwarf Ground Long-jawed Spider builds webs so small and fine that they're often overlooked by naturalists - their entire web can fit within the palm of your hand!

children.description: Long-jawed Orbweavers are a family of spiders known for their distinctive elongated jaws (chelicerae) and ability to construct orb-shaped webs. These spiders are typically found near water sources like streams, ponds, and wetlands, where they build their circular webs to catch flying insects. The family includes both web-building species and some that have adapted to hunting without webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These spiders are easily recognized by their notably long, projecting jaws that extend forward from their head. Unlike typical orbweavers, many species in this family build their webs at an angle or horizontally rather than vertically.
children.funFact: Stretch spiders (Tetragnatha) can extend their front legs forward and rear legs backward to stretch their bodies into a thin line, making them nearly invisible when resting along plant stems or grass blades.

children.name: Agelenidae
Coras
children.description: Coras is a genus of funnel weaver spiders that create distinctive sheet webs with funnel-shaped retreats where they hide and wait for prey. These medium-sized spiders are commonly found in woodlands, gardens, and around human structures throughout New England. They are fast runners and excellent hunters that dart out from their funnel retreats to capture insects that stumble onto their horizontal web sheets.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Coras spiders can be distinguished from other funnel weavers by their relatively robust build and the presence of spurs (modified spines) on their legs, which is particularly noticeable in some species like the Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver.
children.funFact: Unlike orb weavers that rebuild their webs daily, Coras spiders are excellent housekeepers that maintain and repair the same funnel web for weeks or even months, continuously adding silk to expand their hunting grounds.

children.name: Agelenopsis
children.description: Grass spiders are medium-sized spiders that build distinctive funnel-shaped webs in grass, bushes, and other vegetation. These webs have a flat sheet portion where prey gets trapped and a tubular retreat where the spider waits to ambush its victims. All members of this genus are fast runners with excellent eyesight for detecting movement across their webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike orb weavers that build circular webs, grass spiders create horizontal sheet webs with a distinctive funnel-shaped retreat at one end. They can be distinguished from similar funnel-web spiders by their longer legs and more slender build.
children.funFact: Grass spiders don't use sticky silk to catch prey - instead, they rely on the tangled texture of their sheet webs to trip up insects, then rush out at lightning speed to capture their confused victims.

children.name: Wadotes
children.description: Wadotes is a small genus of harvestmen (daddy longlegs) found in North America. These arachnids are characterized by their long, delicate legs and compact oval bodies, and they're typically found in forest habitats where they hunt for small prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wadotes species can be distinguished from other harvestmen by their relatively robust chelicerae (mouthparts) and the distinctive spines or projections on their leg segments.
children.funFact: Despite being called daddy longlegs, Wadotes harvestmen are not spiders at all - they belong to a separate order of arachnids and cannot produce silk or venom.

children.name: Tegenaria
children.description: Tegenaria is a genus of medium to large spiders that build distinctive funnel-shaped webs in corners and crevices. These spiders are known for their long legs and fast movements, often startling people when they dart across floors or walls in homes and buildings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike orb weavers that create circular webs, Tegenaria spiders construct flat sheet webs with a funnel-shaped retreat at one end where they wait for prey.
children.funFact: Barn Funnel Weavers can live for several years, which is unusually long for spiders, and the same individual may occupy the same web location for months at a time.

children.description: Funnel weavers are spiders that build distinctive sheet webs with a funnel-shaped retreat at one corner where they hide and wait for prey. These medium-sized spiders are fast runners with long legs and typically have brownish coloration with subtle patterns that help them blend into their surroundings. You'll often find their webs stretched across grass, shrubs, or in the corners of buildings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike orb weavers that build circular webs, funnel weavers create flat, sheet-like webs with a distinctive funnel or tube-shaped hiding spot. Their webs don't have the sticky spiral threads of orb webs, instead relying on the spider's speed to catch prey that lands on the sheet.
children.funFact: Grass spiders can run across their webs at speeds up to 1.7 feet per second - that's incredibly fast for such a small creature!

children.name: Philodromidae
Philodromus
children.description: Running Crab Spiders are active hunters that combine the sideways movement typical of crab spiders with impressive speed and agility. Unlike their sit-and-wait cousins, these spiders actively chase down their prey on flowers, leaves, and bark surfaces. They have flattened bodies and long legs that allow them to scuttle quickly in any direction when hunting or escaping danger.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These spiders can be distinguished from other crab spiders by their more elongated bodies and their habit of running rapidly rather than sitting motionless while hunting. They also tend to be smaller and more slender than the chunky flower crab spiders most people are familiar with.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'crab spiders,' Running Crab Spiders are actually more closely related to wolf spiders than to the classic flower crab spiders, and some species can change color to match their surroundings!

children.name: Tibellus
children.description: Slender Crab Spiders are elongated arachnids that get their name from their distinctive thin, stretched-out body shape that sets them apart from typical round-bodied crab spiders. These spiders are excellent hunters that don't build webs, instead relying on their speed and agility to chase down prey. They're often found on plants and flowers where they ambush insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crab spiders that are typically wide and compact, Tibellus spiders have notably elongated, narrow bodies that make them look almost stick-like. Their legs are also proportionally longer, giving them a more spider-like appearance compared to their crab-shaped relatives.
children.funFact: These spiders can stretch their bodies out along plant stems and grass blades, making themselves nearly invisible as they wait motionless for hours to ambush unsuspecting prey.

children.name: Thanatus
children.description: Thanatus is a genus of crab spiders known for their distinctive lance-shaped markings on their abdomens, which give them their common name of lance-backed crab spiders. These medium-sized spiders are active hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead relying on their speed and agility to chase down insects. They're typically found on the ground, under stones, or in low vegetation where they hunt for small arthropods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other crab spiders that are ambush predators, Thanatus spiders are active hunters that pursue their prey. Their elongated bodies and prominent lance-shaped abdominal markings make them easily distinguishable from the more compact, flower-dwelling crab spiders.
children.funFact: The Cricket Thief Spider earned its common name from its habit of stealing prey from spider webs, boldly walking into other spiders' webs to snatch caught insects before making a quick escape.

children.description: Running crab spiders are active hunters that don't build webs to catch their prey. Like other crab spiders, they can move sideways and backwards as well as forward, but unlike their sit-and-wait cousins, these spiders actively chase down their meals. They have relatively long legs and are built for speed and agility.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crab spider families that ambush prey from flowers or other hiding spots, running crab spiders are mobile hunters that actively pursue their victims. They have longer, more slender legs than typical crab spiders and lack the extremely flattened body shape of their sedentary relatives.
children.funFact: Some running crab spiders can change color over several days to match their surroundings, shifting between white, yellow, and green to blend in with the flowers and foliage where they hunt.

children.name: Clubionidae
Clubiona
children.description: Leafcurling Sac Spiders are small to medium-sized hunting spiders that get their name from their habit of creating silken retreats by curling leaves together or hiding in cracks and crevices. These nocturnal hunters don't build webs to catch prey, but instead actively search for insects and other small arthropods during the night. During the day, they rest in their characteristic silken sacs tucked away in protected spots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike web-building spiders, Clubiona species are wandering hunters that construct tubular silk retreats rather than prey-catching webs. They can be distinguished from other sac spiders by their relatively robust build and the way they curl leaves or use natural crevices for their daytime shelters.
children.funFact: These spiders are excellent mothers - females guard their egg sacs inside their silk retreats and will aggressively defend them from potential threats, even sacrificing their own safety for their offspring.

children.name: Elaver
children.description: Elaver is a small genus of sac spiders, with only one species found in New England - the white sac spider. These spiders are part of the broader sac spider family, known for building silken retreats or 'sacs' where they rest during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Elaver spiders are distinguished from other sac spiders by their specific body proportions and leg arrangements. The white sac spider has a pale, yellowish-white coloration that helps separate it from similar species.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'white' sac spiders, Elaver excepta can actually appear pale yellow or cream-colored, and they're active nighttime hunters that abandon their daytime silk retreats to prowl for prey.

children.description: Sac spiders are small to medium-sized hunting spiders that build silken retreats or 'sacs' where they rest during the day. They are active nighttime hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead roaming to capture insects and other small arthropods. Most species have elongated bodies and relatively long legs that help them move quickly across various surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike web-building spiders, sac spiders create tubular silk retreats in curled leaves, under bark, or in corners where they hide during daylight hours. They have two prominent claws on each foot and typically hold their front legs extended forward when at rest.
children.funFact: Some sac spiders are accomplished leaf architects - they use silk to curl up leaves into protective tubes, essentially creating their own custom shelters by reshaping living foliage.

children.name: Pholcidae
Pholcus
children.description: Common Cellar Spiders are delicate, long-legged spiders that you've likely encountered in the corners of basements, garages, and other quiet indoor spaces. These spiders build messy, irregular webs and are known for their distinctive habit of rapidly vibrating or bouncing in their webs when disturbed. All members of this genus share similar body proportions with extremely long, thin legs relative to their small bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other long-legged spiders, Pholcus spiders have a distinctive cylindrical abdomen and hold their legs in a characteristic relaxed position. They can be distinguished from similar-looking harvestmen (daddy longlegs) because they have a clear separation between their cephalothorax and abdomen.
children.funFact: When threatened, these spiders will violently shake their entire web so fast they become a blur, earning them the nickname 'vibrating spiders' - this behavior is thought to confuse predators and make the spider harder to catch.

children.name: Spermophora
children.description: Dwarf cellar spiders are tiny spiders that live in dark, humid places like basements, cellars, and caves. They are much smaller than their common cellar spider cousins, with bodies that are notably short and compact. These spiders build small, irregular webs in corners and crevices where they catch small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike regular cellar spiders with their long, skinny bodies and extremely long legs, dwarf cellar spiders have short, rounded bodies and proportionally shorter legs. They also have only six eyes arranged in a distinctive pattern, rather than the eight eyes most spiders possess.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'cellar spiders,' these tiny arachnids are more commonly found in natural cave environments and only occasionally venture into human-made spaces like basements.

children.name: Holocnemus
children.description: Holocnemus is a genus of cellar spiders known for their extremely long, thin legs and small bodies. These spiders are skilled web builders that construct irregular, tangled webs in dark, humid spaces like basements, caves, and other sheltered areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Holocnemus spiders can be distinguished from other cellar spiders by their distinctive marbled or mottled body patterns and their preference for building webs in the darkest corners of structures.
children.funFact: When threatened, Holocnemus spiders vibrate rapidly in their webs, creating a blur that makes them nearly impossible for predators to target accurately.

children.name: Crossopriza
children.description: Crossopriza is a genus of cellar spiders known for their extremely long, thin legs and small bodies. These spiders are commonly found in dark, humid spaces like basements, caves, and other sheltered areas where they build irregular webs to catch small flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cellar spiders, Crossopriza species have distinctively long tails or projections on their abdomens, which is where the common name 'tailed cellar spider' comes from.
children.funFact: When threatened, these spiders will rapidly vibrate in their webs, creating a blurring effect that makes them nearly impossible to see clearly - a defense mechanism called 'whirling.'

children.description: Cellar spiders are delicate, long-legged spiders that are commonly found in dark, quiet spaces like basements, caves, and corners of buildings. They build loose, irregular webs and are known for their distinctive behavior of vibrating rapidly in their webs when disturbed. These spiders have small bodies relative to their extremely long, thin legs, giving them a fragile appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other web-building spiders, cellar spiders have exceptionally long, thin legs that can be 5-6 times longer than their body length. When threatened, they vibrate so rapidly in their webs that they become a blur, earning them the nickname 'vibrating spiders.'
children.funFact: Despite the common myth that cellar spiders are the most venomous spiders but have fangs too small to bite humans, they actually have very mild venom and can bite people, though their bites are harmless and rarely occur.

children.name: Dolomedidae
Dolomedes
children.description: Fishing spiders are large, semi-aquatic spiders that live near water sources like ponds, streams, and marshes throughout New England. These impressive hunters can walk on water's surface and even dive underwater to catch prey, using their long legs to detect vibrations on the water. They're among the largest spiders you'll encounter in the region, with leg spans that can reach 3-4 inches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other large spiders, fishing spiders have water-repellent hairs that allow them to walk on water without sinking. They also have excellent eyesight and can detect movement both above and below the water's surface.
children.funFact: Female fishing spiders are devoted mothers who carry their egg sacs in their jaws and later carry hundreds of tiny spiderlings on their backs until they're ready to hunt on their own.

children.description: Dolomedidae is a family of large, semi-aquatic spiders commonly known as fishing spiders. These impressive arachnids are closely associated with water environments like ponds, streams, and wetlands, where they hunt for prey both on the water's surface and underwater.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most spiders, fishing spiders can walk on water using surface tension and even dive underwater to catch prey, staying submerged for up to 30 minutes by trapping air bubbles around their bodies.
children.funFact: Female fishing spiders are devoted mothers who carry their egg sacs in their jaws and later allow hundreds of spiderlings to ride on their backs until they're ready to live independently.

children.name: Anyphaenidae
Anyphaena
children.description: Anyphaena is a genus of small, fast-moving spiders commonly known as ghost spiders. These nocturnal hunters are typically pale colored and have relatively long legs compared to their body size, making them well-adapted for quick movement across plant surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike web-building spiders, Anyphaena spiders are active hunters that don't construct webs to catch prey. They can be distinguished from similar hunting spiders by their characteristic pale coloration and their habit of running quickly when disturbed.
children.funFact: Ghost spiders got their common name because of their pale, almost translucent appearance and their ability to seemingly vanish by moving incredibly quickly when a light is shined on them at night.

children.name: Hibana
children.description: Hibana is a genus of small, pale spiders commonly known as ghost spiders due to their translucent, whitish appearance. These delicate spiders are active hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead stalking and pouncing on small insects. They are typically found in gardens, leaf litter, and under rocks or logs where they hunt at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ghost spiders in the genus Hibana can be distinguished from other small hunting spiders by their pale, almost transparent coloration and their relatively long, thin legs. They also have distinctive eye arrangements and lack the robust build of jumping spiders or wolf spiders.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'ghost spiders,' Hibana species are very much alive and active - they got their spooky name because their pale, translucent bodies can appear almost invisible against light-colored surfaces.

children.name: Wulfila
children.description: Wulfila is a genus of ghost spiders, which are small, pale-colored hunting spiders that don't build webs to catch prey. These spiders are active predators that rely on their speed and agility to chase down small insects and other tiny arthropods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the genus Wulfila are characterized by their exceptionally long legs relative to their body size and their translucent, ghostly appearance that gives the group its common name.
children.funFact: The Long-legged Ghost Spider can run so quickly across surfaces that it almost seems to disappear, earning its 'ghost' nickname from its ability to vanish from sight in the blink of an eye.

children.name: Arachosia
children.description: Arachosia is a small genus of tiny jumping spiders known for their remarkable ability to leap many times their own body length when hunting prey or escaping danger. These miniature predators have excellent eyesight and are active hunters that stalk their insect prey rather than building webs to catch them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arachosia spiders can be distinguished from other jumping spiders by their particularly small size and distinctive eye arrangement, with their large forward-facing eyes giving them almost comical expressions.
children.funFact: Despite being smaller than a pinky nail, Arachosia spiders can jump up to 40 times their own body length - equivalent to a human jumping the length of two football fields!

children.name: Lupettiana
children.description: Lupettiana is a genus of marine gastropod mollusks, commonly known as sea snails. These small mollusks live in marine environments and are characterized by their spiral shells and soft bodies that can retract inside for protection.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their specific shell shape and sculpture patterns that differ from other marine snail genera in the same family.
children.funFact: The genus name Lupettiana was named after a malacologist (scientist who studies mollusks) to honor their contributions to understanding marine snail diversity.

children.description: Ghost spiders are small, pale-colored hunting spiders that actively stalk their prey rather than building webs to catch food. They are typically found on plants, tree bark, and under stones, where their light coloration helps them blend in with their surroundings. These nimble spiders are most active at night when they hunt for small insects and other tiny arthropods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ghost spiders can be identified by their relatively long legs, pale yellow to whitish coloration, and the absence of a catching web. Unlike web-building spiders, they have excellent eyesight and rely on speed and stealth to capture prey.
children.funFact: Ghost spiders got their common name from their pale, almost translucent appearance and their habit of quickly disappearing into cracks and crevices when disturbed, seeming to vanish like phantoms.

children.name: Corinnidae
Castianeira
children.description: Ant-mimic sac spiders in the genus Castianeira are master impersonators that have evolved to look and behave remarkably like ants. These small, active spiders have elongated bodies, constricted waists, and often wave their front legs like antennae to complete their disguise. They're part of the sac spider family and are commonly found running around on the ground or low vegetation during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sac spiders, Castianeira species have distinctly ant-like proportions with narrow, constricted abdomens and often metallic or iridescent coloration. They're also much more active during daylight hours compared to their mostly nocturnal sac spider relatives.
children.funFact: These spiders are so convincing in their ant mimicry that they can often be found running alongside real ant trails without being detected by the ants themselves!

children.name: Myrmecotypus
children.description: Myrmecotypus is a genus of small beetles that are masters of disguise, mimicking ants in their appearance and behavior. These tiny insects have evolved to look and move like ants, which helps protect them from predators who might avoid attacking what they think is a well-defended ant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true ants, these beetles have the characteristic beetle body structure with hardened wing covers, but their narrow waist and quick movements make them excellent ant mimics.
children.funFact: The name 'Myrmecotypus' literally means 'ant-type,' reflecting their remarkable ability to fool both predators and even experienced naturalists into thinking they're actually ants!

children.description: Ground and Ant-mimic Sac Spiders are swift-moving hunters that actively chase down their prey rather than building webs to catch food. Many species in this family have evolved to look and move remarkably like ants, which helps protect them from predators and allows them to get close to ant prey. They're typically small, dark-colored spiders with slender bodies and long legs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most spiders, many corinnids have a distinctly ant-like appearance with constricted abdomens and jerky movements that mimic ant behavior. They also have relatively long, thin legs compared to their body size and are exceptionally fast runners.
children.funFact: Some ant-mimic sac spiders are such convincing mimics that they can walk right through colonies of ants without being detected, allowing them to hunt the very insects they're pretending to be!

children.name: Mimetidae
Mimetus
children.description: Cannibal spiders are tiny predators that specialize in hunting other spiders rather than insects. These small arachnids actively seek out spider webs, where they carefully approach their prey and deliver a venomous bite. They're sometimes called pirate spiders because they essentially 'steal' prey from other spiders' webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most spiders that build webs to catch flying insects, cannibal spiders are active hunters that specifically target other spiders as their primary food source. They have specialized front legs adapted for grasping spider prey and can be identified by their small size and spider-hunting behavior.
children.funFact: Cannibal spiders can mimic the vibrations of trapped insects in other spiders' webs, luring the web owner close enough to become the meal instead of the hunter.

children.name: Ero
children.description: Pirate spiders are tiny specialized hunters that prey exclusively on other spiders, earning their name through their predatory lifestyle. These small arachnids have evolved unique hunting strategies to capture and feed on spiders that are often larger than themselves. They represent one of nature's most specialized spider-eating specialists.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pirate spiders can be distinguished from other small spiders by their distinctive hunting behavior and their specialized front legs, which are adapted for grasping prey spiders. They also have a characteristic way of approaching webs and manipulating the silk to lure their spider victims.
children.funFact: Pirate spiders will actually pluck the strands of other spiders' webs to mimic the vibrations of trapped prey, tricking the web's owner into approaching close enough to be captured and eaten.

children.description: Pirate spiders are specialized hunters that prey almost exclusively on other spiders, earning their swashbuckling name through their predatory lifestyle. These small to medium-sized spiders have evolved unique hunting strategies, often invading other spiders' webs to capture and eat the web builders. They are considered beneficial predators that help control spider populations in their ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pirate spiders can be identified by their distinctive leg spines arranged in rows and their habit of hunting other spiders rather than typical prey like insects. They also have relatively robust front legs adapted for grasping their spider prey.
children.funFact: Some pirate spiders are so specialized that they mimic the vibrations of trapped insects in other spiders' webs, luring the web owner close enough to become the meal instead of the hunter.

children.name: Phrurolithidae
Phrurotimpus
children.description: Phrurotimpus is a genus of small, ground-dwelling spiders that are part of the ant-mimic spider family. These tiny spiders are active hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead roaming through leaf litter and low vegetation in search of small insects and other tiny arthropods. They're typically found in wooded areas and are most active during warmer months.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished by their small size (usually less than 3mm), elongated bodies, and relatively long legs that give them a somewhat ant-like appearance. They have distinctive eye arrangements and lack the web-spinning behavior of many other spider families.
children.funFact: Despite being called ant-mimic spiders, Phrurotimpus species don't actually look much like ants - the 'ant-mimic' name comes from their ground-dwelling lifestyle and active hunting behavior rather than their physical appearance.

children.name: Scotinella
children.description: Scotinella is a small genus of tiny ground-dwelling spiders that are part of the sheetweb weaver family. These diminutive arachnids are typically found in leaf litter, under stones, or in other dark, moist microhabitats on the forest floor. Both New England species are quite small and can be challenging to spot without careful observation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Scotinella spiders can be distinguished from other sheetweb weavers by their very small size and specific genital structure visible under magnification. They have a relatively compact body shape and tend to be pale or darkly colored depending on the species.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Scotinella spiders are active hunters that don't rely on webs to catch prey, instead pursuing even smaller invertebrates through the maze of decomposing leaves on the forest floor.
