children.description: Guardstone Spiders are small, ground-dwelling hunting spiders that actively pursue their prey rather than building webs. These compact spiders typically have dark coloration and robust bodies, making them well-suited for life among leaf litter and under stones. They are primarily nocturnal hunters that feed on small insects and other tiny arthropods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other hunting spiders, Guardstone Spiders have distinctively shortened spinnerets and often display unique patterns of spines on their legs. Their compact, somewhat flattened body shape helps distinguish them from similar-looking ground spiders.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, Guardstone Spiders are fierce predators that can take down prey larger than themselves, earning their 'guardstone' name from their habit of lurking motionless under rocks like tiny sentinels.

children.name: Cicurinidae
Cicurina
children.description: Cicurina is a genus of small, ground-dwelling spiders commonly known as cave spiders or sheet web spiders. These tiny hunters build delicate sheet webs near the ground in dark, moist places like caves, basements, and under rocks or logs. They're part of the funnel weaver family and are found throughout North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cicurina spiders are distinguished by their pale coloration, small size (usually less than 6mm), and preference for cave-like environments. Unlike other funnel weavers, they build horizontal sheet webs rather than funnel-shaped retreats.
children.funFact: Many Cicurina species have evolved to live exclusively in caves, with some losing their eyesight entirely and developing enhanced sensory abilities to navigate in complete darkness.

children.description: Cicurinid spiders are small to medium-sized hunting spiders that build simple sheet webs or funnel-like retreats rather than the classic orb webs many people associate with spiders. They are typically found in leaf litter, under rocks, in caves, or other sheltered spots where they wait to ambush small insects and other prey. Most species in this family are brownish or grayish in color, helping them blend into their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cicurinid spiders can be distinguished from other spider families by their eye arrangement, which forms two curved rows, and their relatively long legs compared to their body size. Unlike many web-building spiders, they don't create sticky capture webs but instead rely on speed and stealth to catch prey.
children.funFact: Some cicurinid spiders are among the few spider species that have successfully colonized cave environments, with certain species living their entire lives in complete darkness and developing enhanced sensory abilities to navigate and hunt without sight.

children.name: Hahniidae
Neoantistea
children.description: Neoantistea is a small genus of sheet web spiders found in New England's forests and woodlands. These spiders are known for their distinctive comb-like structures on their tails and their hooked chelicerae (mouthparts). They build small sheet webs close to the ground among leaf litter and low vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their characteristic comb-tailed appearance and thick, hooked chelicerae that give them their common name. They are generally small, agile spiders with relatively robust builds compared to other sheet web spiders.
children.funFact: The 'thick hooks' that give these spiders part of their common name are actually specialized mouthparts that help them handle prey more effectively in their ground-level hunting environment.

children.name: Hahnia
children.description: Hahnia is a genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that build delicate, horizontal webs close to the ground. These small spiders are part of the larger family of sheet web weavers and are known for their intricate web-building abilities despite their diminutive size.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hahnia spiders can be distinguished from other sheet weavers by their distinctive web structure that includes both a horizontal sheet and a three-dimensional tangle above it, creating a complex trap for small flying insects.
children.funFact: Despite being less than 3mm in body length, Hahnia spiders can construct webs that are many times larger than themselves, sometimes spanning several inches across.

children.name: Antistea
children.description: Antistea is a small genus of ferns that includes just one species found in New England. These ferns are part of the larger wood fern family and are characterized by their delicate, lacy fronds that grow in small clusters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Antistea can be distinguished from other wood ferns by its smaller size and more delicate appearance, with thin, papery fronds that have a distinctive brownish color when mature.
children.funFact: The genus name Antistea comes from Greek words meaning 'opposite crown,' referring to the arrangement of the spore-bearing structures on the underside of the fronds.

children.description: Comb-tailed spiders are small, delicate spiders named for the row of curved bristles (called a calamistrum) on their hind legs that resembles a tiny comb. They use this specialized comb to handle their silk while spinning their webs, creating distinctive woolly or fuzzy-textured capture threads. These spiders are typically found in leaf litter, under logs, or in other ground-level habitats where they build small sheet webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The defining feature is the calamistrum - a row of curved bristles on the metatarsus of the fourth leg that acts like a comb for processing silk. This comb works together with a spinning plate called a cribellum to produce hackled silk that appears woolly rather than smooth.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'comb-tailed' spiders, the comb is actually located on their legs, not their abdomen - they use this silk comb like a tiny spinning wheel to create fuzzy capture threads that can snag the fine hairs of small insects.

children.name: Amaurobiidae
Amaurobius
children.description: Lace web spiders are medium-sized spiders that create distinctive woolly, sheet-like webs with a lacy appearance. They are typically dark-colored spiders that build their webs in crevices, under bark, or in similar protected locations. These spiders are active hunters that wait at the edge of their webs to detect prey caught in the sticky silk.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical orb weavers, lace web spiders create flat, sheet-like webs with a characteristic fuzzy, woolly texture rather than the classic wheel-shaped webs. Their webs have a distinctive blue-gray sheen and hackled band of silk that gives them their lacy appearance.
children.funFact: Female lace web spiders practice matriphagy - the young spiders actually eat their mother after hatching, which provides them with essential nutrients for their early development.

children.name: Callobius
children.description: Callobius is a genus of spiders known as laceweavers, named for the delicate, lace-like webs they create. These spiders are part of the hacklemesh weaver family and are typically found in cool, moist environments like under rocks, logs, or in leaf litter. They are relatively small, dark-colored spiders that prefer to stay hidden during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Callobius spiders can be identified by their distinctive web structure, which combines a sheet-like base with sticky capture threads that create a lacy appearance. Unlike many other web-building spiders, they incorporate special silk called hackled band silk that has a woolly, bluish appearance.
children.funFact: The hackled band silk produced by Callobius spiders is created using a special spinning organ called a cribellum, which combs the silk into extremely fine fibers that can trap prey without being sticky.

children.description: Hackledmesh weavers are small to medium-sized spiders known for their distinctive webs made of woolly, bluish silk that has a fuzzy, hackled appearance. They create irregular sheet webs or funnel webs in crevices, under rocks, or in bark crevices where they wait to capture prey. These spiders are most active at night and are commonly found in cool, moist environments throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets hackledmesh weavers apart is their unique cribellum, a specialized spinning organ that produces the characteristic hackled or woolly silk fibers. This gives their webs a distinctly fuzzy, blue-tinged appearance that's quite different from the smooth, clear webs of most other spider families.
children.funFact: The hackled silk produced by these spiders is so fine and woolly that it can actually trap prey without being sticky - the fuzzy fibers simply tangle up insects like microscopic velcro!

children.name: Cheiracanthiidae
Cheiracanthium
children.description: Longlegged Sac Spiders are small to medium-sized hunting spiders known for their distinctively long, thin legs and pale coloration. They build silken retreats or 'sacs' in rolled leaves, under bark, or in corners of buildings where they rest during the day. These active nighttime hunters don't spin webs to catch prey, instead roaming to hunt small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their exceptionally long, slender legs and pale yellow to greenish coloration make them easy to distinguish from other sac spiders. They also have distinctive dark-tipped chelicerae (mouthparts) that are often visible even from a distance.
children.funFact: These spiders are among the most common house spiders in New England and are responsible for many spider bites attributed to more dangerous species, though their bites are generally harmless to humans.

children.name: Strotarchus
children.description: Strotarchus is a small genus of marine fish found in cold Atlantic waters. These bottom-dwelling fish are characterized by their elongated bodies and ability to live in deep ocean environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished by their distinctive body shape and specialized adaptations for deep-water living.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Strotarchus piscatorius, is rarely encountered due to its preference for deep offshore waters.

children.description: Long-legged Sac Spiders are small to medium-sized hunting spiders known for their notably long, slender legs and pale coloration. They build silken retreats or sacs in rolled leaves, under bark, or in corners of buildings where they rest during the day before emerging to hunt at night. These active predators don't build webs to catch prey, instead relying on their speed and agility to chase down small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their exceptionally long, thin legs relative to their body size make them easy to identify, along with their habit of constructing tubular silk retreats rather than orb webs. Most species have a pale yellow or greenish coloration that helps distinguish them from other sac spider families.
children.funFact: Some Long-legged Sac Spiders are among the few spiders whose bites can be medically significant to humans, though serious reactions are rare and typically mild compared to more dangerous spider species.

children.name: Uloboridae
Uloborus
children.description: Feather-legged spiders are small orb weavers that get their name from the distinctive feathery hairs on their legs that help them handle their sticky silk. These spiders are unique among orb weavers because they lack venom glands entirely, instead wrapping their prey extensively in silk to subdue them. They build classic circular webs but use a special technique involving their feathery leg hairs to avoid getting stuck in their own sticky traps.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb weaver spiders, feather-legged spiders have no venom glands and rely solely on silk to capture and kill their prey. Their legs are covered in distinctive feathery or plume-like hairs that are easily visible and help distinguish them from other small web-building spiders.
children.funFact: Feather-legged spiders are living fossils - they represent one of the most ancient lineages of orb weavers and may show us what the very first web-spinning spiders looked like millions of years ago.

children.name: Hyptiotes
children.description: Triangle Web Spiders are unique orb weavers that create distinctive triangular webs rather than the typical circular patterns of their relatives. These small spiders hold their incomplete webs under tension, using their bodies as a spring-loaded trap to capture flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb weavers, Triangle Web Spiders build only a triangular sector of web with just 3-4 radial threads and connecting spirals, creating a pie-slice shaped snare.
children.funFact: When prey hits the web, the spider releases its grip and springs forward, wrapping the victim in additional silk threads while the web collapses around it.

children.name: Octonoba
children.description: Octonoba is a small genus of orb weaver spiders known for building circular webs to catch flying insects. These spiders are part of the large family Araneidae, which includes many of the classic wheel-shaped web builders we commonly see in gardens and forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Octonoba spiders are distinguished from other orb weavers by their relatively small size and specific web architecture patterns, though detailed identification often requires examination of their reproductive structures.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Octonoba sinensis, is actually native to Asia and represents a relatively recent arrival to North America, likely introduced through human commerce.

children.description: Hackled Orbweavers are a unique family of spiders that create circular webs using a special fuzzy silk called 'hackled band.' Unlike most spiders, they don't have venom glands and instead subdue their prey by wrapping them tightly in silk. These spiders are found throughout New England but are often overlooked due to their small size and cryptic behavior.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These are the only spiders that produce hackled band silk, which appears as a fuzzy, woolly thread that helps entangle prey. They are also the only orb weaver spiders that completely lack venom, making them harmless hunters that rely entirely on silk manipulation.
children.funFact: Triangle Web Spiders can collapse their triangular webs in an instant by releasing tension, catapulting surprised insects directly into the waiting spider!

children.name: Oxyopidae
Oxyopes
children.description: Grass lynx spiders are active hunters that live among tall grasses and low vegetation, where they stalk and pounce on their prey like miniature cats. These agile spiders have long, spiny legs that help them move quickly through grass stems and leaves. Unlike web-building spiders, they rely on their keen eyesight and speed to catch flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Grass lynx spiders can be identified by their elongated bodies, prominent forward-facing eyes, and legs covered in distinctive black spines. Their front legs are noticeably longer than their back legs, giving them a distinctive stretched appearance.
children.funFact: These spiders can leap several times their body length to catch flying prey, earning their 'lynx' name from their cat-like hunting pounce.

children.name: Peucetia
children.description: Green Lynx Spiders are active hunting spiders known for their bright green coloration and long, spiny legs. These agile predators don't build webs to catch prey, but instead rely on their excellent vision and quick reflexes to ambush insects on plants and flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be identified by their vibrant green body color, elongated legs covered in prominent spines, and their habit of sitting motionless on vegetation waiting for prey to come within striking distance.
children.funFact: Female Green Lynx Spiders are protective mothers that guard their egg sacs and can actually spit venom up to 8 inches to defend their young from threats.

children.description: Lynx spiders are active hunting spiders that rely on their excellent eyesight and quick reflexes to catch prey, rather than building webs. They have long, spiny legs that help them move quickly through vegetation, and they're often found hunting on plants and flowers during the day. These spiders get their name from their cat-like hunting behavior and alert, forward-facing eyes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lynx spiders can be identified by their distinctive leg spines arranged in multiple rows, their relatively large forward-facing eyes, and their habit of hunting actively on plants rather than in webs.
children.funFact: Green lynx spiders can actually spit venom up to 8 inches to defend themselves, making them one of the few spiders that can use their venom as a projectile weapon!

children.name: Dictynidae
Nopalityna
children.description: Nopalityna is a small genus of sheet weaver spiders in the family Linyphiidae. These are tiny spiders that create delicate horizontal sheet webs to catch small flying insects. They are part of the large group of spiders commonly called money spiders or dwarf spiders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive web structure, which forms wide ribbon-like sheets rather than the typical dome or bowl shapes seen in many other sheet weavers.
children.funFact: The name Nopalityna comes from the Nahuatl word 'nopal' meaning prickly pear cactus, though these spiders are found far from desert environments and prefer moist habitats.

children.name: Emblyna
children.description: Emblyna is a genus of small funnel-web spiders that build sheet webs with funnel-shaped retreats where they hide and wait for prey. These spiders are part of the funnel weaver family and are known for their fast movements when hunting or escaping danger.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Emblyna spiders can be distinguished from other funnel weavers by their relatively small size and specific web construction patterns. They build flatter, more horizontal sheet webs compared to the more vertical funnel webs of many related species.
children.funFact: Despite being called funnel-web spiders, Emblyna species are completely harmless to humans and actually help control pest insects around homes and gardens.

children.name: Arethyna
children.description: Arethyna is a small genus of orb weaver spiders known for their intricate, mesh-like webs. These tiny spiders are part of the larger orb weaver family and are specialized web builders that create delicate, thread-based structures to catch their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arethyna spiders are distinguished by their flared, mesh-like web construction that differs from the typical circular orb webs of their relatives. They build more three-dimensional, funnel-like structures with interconnected threads.
children.funFact: The Flared Thread Meshweaver gets its name from the distinctive flared shape of its web, which resembles a tiny trumpet made of silk threads.

children.description: Meshweavers are small spiders that create distinctive webs with a bluish, hackled silk that has a woolly or fuzzy appearance. They build irregular sheet webs or cobwebs, often in corners of buildings, under rocks, or among vegetation. These spiders are generally small and inconspicuous, making them easy to overlook despite being relatively common.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The hackled silk produced by their cribellum (a special spinning organ) gives their webs a characteristic bluish, woolly appearance that distinguishes them from the smooth webs of other spider families. This cribellate silk appears fuzzy or mesh-like under magnification.
children.funFact: The hackled silk that gives meshweavers their name is actually thousands of extremely fine fibers that work like velcro to trap prey - insects get tangled in the woolly strands even without sticky glue.

children.name: Pisauridae
Pisaurina
children.description: Pisaurina is a genus of medium to large hunting spiders known as nursery web spiders. These spiders are characterized by their maternal care behavior, where females carry their egg sacs in their jaws and later build protective silk nurseries for their newly hatched spiderlings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other spider families, Pisaurina females actively guard their young by constructing tent-like silk structures called nursery webs where spiderlings can safely develop for their first few days.
children.funFact: Female Pisaurina spiders will carry their large, round egg sacs for weeks, holding them constantly in their chelicerae (jaws) until the eggs are ready to hatch.

children.description: Nursery web spiders are medium to large hunting spiders that don't build webs to catch prey, but instead actively hunt insects and other small creatures. The females are known for their exceptional maternal care - they carry their egg sacs in their jaws and later build protective silk 'nursery tents' for their newly hatched spiderlings. These spiders are often found near water or in tall grass and vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most spiders, nursery web spiders carry their round egg sacs attached to their chelicerae (mouthparts) rather than at the end of their abdomen. They can also be distinguished from similar wolf spiders by their eye arrangement and their habit of resting with their front legs extended forward.
children.funFact: Some nursery web spiders can actually walk on water's surface tension and even dive underwater to catch aquatic prey or escape predators, staying submerged for up to 30 minutes by trapping air bubbles around their body.

children.name: Trachelidae
Trachelas
children.description: Trachelas spiders are medium-sized hunting spiders that don't build webs to catch prey. Instead, they actively search for food at night, using their strong jaws and robust build to overpower insects and other small arthropods. These spiders are part of the sac spider family and often hide in silken retreats during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their notably large, broad heads and prominent forward-facing chelicerae (jaws), which give them a distinctive bull-headed appearance. Their robust front end sets them apart from other sac spiders that typically have more proportional head-to-body ratios.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating appearance with oversized heads and jaws, Trachelas spiders are actually quite docile and rarely bite humans, preferring to flee when disturbed.

children.description: Broad-faced sac spiders are small to medium-sized hunting spiders that don't build webs to catch prey. Instead, they actively search for insects and other small creatures to hunt, often at night. They get their name from their relatively wide, flattened faces compared to other sac spider families.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These spiders can be identified by their broad, flattened front section (cephalothorax) and their habit of building silk retreats or sacs in sheltered spots like under bark or in leaf litter, rather than spinning webs.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'sac spiders,' they're actually active hunters that only use their silk to create protective shelters for resting and molting, not for catching food.

children.name: Scytodidae
Scytodes
children.description: Scytodes is a genus of small, slow-moving spiders known for their unique hunting technique of spitting a sticky substance at their prey. These spiders have distinctively domed, rounded abdomens and relatively long legs compared to their body size. They are typically yellowish or brown in color with darker markings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most spiders that use webs or direct attacks, Scytodes spiders subdue their prey by ejecting a mixture of silk and venom from their fangs with remarkable accuracy. Their enlarged cephalothorax houses special glands that produce this spitting mixture.
children.funFact: Spitting spiders can accurately hit prey from a distance of about 10-20mm by rapidly oscillating their fangs side to side while spitting, creating a zigzag pattern that pins down their victim!

children.description: Spitting spiders are a unique family of small, slow-moving spiders that have developed an extraordinary hunting technique. Instead of building webs or chasing prey, these spiders literally spit a sticky, venomous mixture at their victims from a distance. They are typically pale yellow or brown in color and move very deliberately as they hunt.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other spiders, spitting spiders have modified venom glands that can rapidly eject a zigzag pattern of sticky silk and venom up to 10 body lengths away. They also have a distinctive domed carapace (upper shell) that houses their enlarged venom glands.
children.funFact: A spitting spider can immobilize its prey in just 1/700th of a second by shooting two streams of venomous glue that zigzag back and forth up to 30 times, pinning the victim to the ground before it even knows what happened.

children.name: Atypidae
Sphodros
children.description: Sphodros is a genus of primitive spiders known as purseweb spiders that create distinctive silk tubes extending from underground burrows up tree trunks or walls. These spiders spend most of their lives hidden inside their silk tubes, waiting for prey to walk across the surface. They are relatively large, stocky spiders with powerful fangs that strike downward like those of tarantulas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most spiders, purseweb spiders have fangs that point straight down rather than toward each other, and they construct unique tubular silk retreats that extend above ground. Their robust, cylindrical bodies and primitive features set them apart from more modern spider families.
children.funFact: When prey walks across their silk tube, purseweb spiders bite right through the tube wall from the inside, pull their victim through the hole, then patch up the damage to their tube afterward.

children.description: Purseweb spiders are primitive spiders that construct distinctive silk tubes extending from underground burrows up tree trunks or along the ground. These spiders have downward-pointing fangs and spend most of their lives hidden inside their silk purses, waiting for prey to walk across the tube so they can bite through the silk to capture it.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most spiders, purseweb spiders have fangs that point straight down rather than toward each other, and they are mygalomorphs like tarantulas with two pairs of book lungs instead of one.
children.funFact: When prey walks across their silk tube, purseweb spiders can sense the vibrations and strike upward through the silk wall to grab their meal, then quickly repair the hole in their protective tube.

children.name: Phonognathidae
Zygiella
children.description: Missing-sector orbweb spiders are small to medium-sized spiders that build circular webs with a distinctive twist - they leave one or two sectors of their web incomplete, creating a gap that looks like a missing pie slice. These spiders typically position themselves at the center of their web or hide in a nearby retreat connected to the web by a signal thread. They're commonly found around buildings, bridges, and other human-made structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orbweavers that create complete circular webs, Zygiella spiders deliberately leave sectors of their webs unfinished, creating characteristic gaps. This incomplete web design is their signature trait that makes them easily recognizable among orbweaver spiders.
children.funFact: The missing sectors in their webs aren't a design flaw - they're intentional pathways that allow the spider to quickly escape to its hiding spot when threatened, while still maintaining a signal thread to detect prey caught in the web.

children.description: Leaf-curling Orbweavers are spiders that build the classic circular webs we often think of when we picture spider webs. What makes them special is their habit of hiding in curled leaves, rolled-up plant material, or small retreats near their webs during the day, emerging at night to hunt.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orbweaver families, these spiders typically build webs with a distinctive missing sector - a pie-slice shaped gap in the web where no sticky silk is present.
children.funFact: The missing sector in their webs isn't a mistake - it's actually a clever design that allows the spider to quickly detect vibrations from prey while remaining hidden in their leaf retreat, with one leg stretched along a signal line that runs through the gap.

children.name: Dysderidae
Dysdera
children.description: Dysdera is a genus of specialized hunting spiders that have evolved specifically to prey on woodlice (pill bugs and sow bugs). These medium-sized spiders are easily recognized by their distinctive reddish-brown coloration and unusually large, prominent fangs that help them pierce through their prey's tough armor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have exceptionally large chelicerae (mouthparts) and fangs compared to other spiders of similar size, along with a characteristic reddish-brown cephalothorax and pale yellowish abdomen.
children.funFact: Woodlouse spiders are one of the few spider species that specialize in hunting just one type of prey - they've developed oversized fangs specifically to penetrate the hard exoskeleton of woodlice!

children.description: Woodlouse Hunter Spiders are specialized predators that have evolved specifically to hunt woodlice (pill bugs and sow bugs). These spiders are easily recognized by their distinctive reddish-brown coloration and unusually large, prominent fangs that help them pierce through their prey's tough armor. They are nocturnal hunters that actively seek out woodlice in damp, dark places like under logs, stones, and leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most spiders, Woodlouse Hunter Spiders have only six eyes arranged in a semicircle, rather than the typical eight eyes. Their oversized chelicerae (mouthparts) and fangs are uniquely adapted for penetrating the hard exoskeleton of woodlice.
children.funFact: These spiders are so specialized that they rarely eat anything other than woodlice, making them one of the most dietary-specific spider families in the world.

children.name: Theridiosomatidae
Theridiosoma
children.description: Ray spiders are tiny orb weavers that create some of the most ingenious webs in the spider world. These small spiders build cone-shaped webs with a unique trigger mechanism that allows them to rapidly collapse their web to capture prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical orb weavers with flat circular webs, ray spiders construct cone or funnel-shaped webs with a central trigger line that they hold taut, ready to release at a moment's notice.
children.funFact: Ray spiders are sometimes called "spring-loaded spiders" because they sit at the center of their cone web holding a trigger line, and when prey touches the web, they instantly release the line to collapse the web around their victim like a net.

children.description: Ray orbweavers are tiny spiders that build small, delicate orb webs with distinctive radiating lines that look like the spokes of a wheel. These minute arachnids are among the smallest orb-weaver spiders, typically measuring only 1-3 millimeters in body length. They prefer moist, shaded environments like forest understories where they construct their intricate webs between vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb-weavers, ray orbweavers build webs with very few sticky spiral threads but prominent radiating 'ray' lines that give them their name. Their webs also have a unique cone-shaped or tent-like structure in the center where the spider waits.
children.funFact: Ray orbweavers can actually pull their entire web into a cone shape when prey gets caught, using it like a collapsible trap to quickly subdue insects much larger than themselves.

children.name: Segestriidae
Ariadna
children.description: Tube-web spiders are primitive spiders that construct distinctive silk tubes in crevices, under rocks, or in bark. These spiders have two pairs of book lungs (most modern spiders have only one pair) and downward-pointing fangs that move parallel to each other rather than pinching together. They are sit-and-wait predators that detect prey walking over their tube entrance through vibrations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most modern spiders, tube-web spiders have parallel-moving fangs that strike downward and two pairs of book lungs for breathing. Their tube-shaped webs are also distinctive compared to the orb webs or sheet webs of other spider families.
children.funFact: Tube-web spiders are considered "living fossils" because they retain many primitive characteristics that their ancient spider ancestors had over 300 million years ago.

children.description: Tunnel spiders are a small family of hunting spiders that build distinctive tubular silk retreats in cracks, crevices, or under bark. Unlike web-building spiders that wait in the center of their webs, these spiders hide inside their silk-lined tunnels and dash out to capture prey that ventures too close. They are active hunters that rely on speed and stealth rather than elaborate webs to catch their meals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tunnel spiders can be identified by their six eyes arranged in two rows (most spiders have eight eyes) and their habit of building tube-shaped silk retreats rather than typical webs. Their front legs are notably longer and more robust than their back legs, adapted for quick strikes from their tunnel entrances.
children.funFact: Tunnel spiders are sometimes called 'six-eyed spiders' because they have lost two of the eight eyes that most spiders possess, likely as an adaptation to their lifestyle of hunting from dark retreats where vision is less important than vibration detection.

children.name: Sparassidae
Heteropoda
children.description: Giant Huntsman Spiders are large, fast-moving spiders known for their impressive leg spans and hunting prowess. These spiders don't build webs to catch prey, but instead actively hunt down insects and other small creatures using their speed and agility. They get their name from their hunting behavior and their ability to move quickly across surfaces in pursuit of food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike web-building spiders, huntsman spiders have legs that extend sideways like a crab and are built for rapid movement rather than web construction. They are considerably larger than most house spiders, with leg spans that can reach several inches across.
children.funFact: The Pantropical Huntsman Spider found in New England is actually a world traveler that likely arrived here by hitchhiking on ships and cargo from tropical regions around the globe.

children.description: Huntsman spiders are large, fast-moving spiders that don't build webs to catch prey. Instead, they actively hunt down their food, using their speed and agility to chase insects and other small creatures. These spiders have flattened bodies and long legs that extend sideways like a crab.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most spiders, huntsman spiders have legs that extend sideways from their body rather than underneath, giving them their characteristic crab-like appearance and allowing them to move sideways quickly.
children.funFact: The Giant Huntsman Spider has the largest leg span of any spider in the world, reaching up to 12 inches across - about the size of a dinner plate!

children.name: Antrodiaetidae
Antrodiaetus
children.description: Antrodiaetus is a genus of primitive mygalomorph spiders commonly known as folding-door spiders or turret spiders. These spiders are among the most ancient spider lineages in North America, closely related to tarantulas but much smaller in size. They construct distinctive burrows in the ground with hinged, cork-like doors that they use to ambush prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other trapdoor spiders, Antrodiaetus spiders have a unique folding door mechanism where the burrow entrance folds inward rather than opening outward like a traditional trapdoor. Their front legs are particularly robust and equipped with specialized spines for digging.
children.funFact: These ancient spiders can live for over a decade and rarely venture more than a few inches from their burrow entrance, making them one of the most sedentary spider species in New England.

children.description: Foldingdoor spiders are primitive mygalomorph spiders that build distinctive burrows with hinged, cork-like doors that fold inward when opened. These medium-sized spiders are closely related to trapdoor spiders and represent an ancient lineage that has remained relatively unchanged for millions of years. They are secretive ground-dwellers that spend most of their lives hidden in their silk-lined burrows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical trapdoor spiders, foldingdoor spiders create doors that fold inward rather than opening outward on a hinge. They also have a more primitive body structure with less specialized spinning organs compared to most other mygalomorphs.
children.funFact: Foldingdoor spiders are considered living fossils - their body plan and behavior have remained virtually unchanged for over 100 million years, making them older than the dinosaurs!

children.name: Filistatidae
Kukulcania
children.description: Kukulcania is a genus of cribellate spiders known for building distinctive funnel webs with woolly, bluish silk. These medium to large spiders are part of the funnel weaver family and are commonly found around human structures like houses, barns, and sheds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other funnel weavers, Kukulcania spiders produce a distinctive bluish, woolly silk using specialized spinning organs called cribellar combs. Their webs have a characteristic messy, cotton-like appearance rather than the neat sheet webs of other funnel weavers.
children.funFact: The Southern House Spider shows extreme sexual dimorphism - females can live up to 8 years and grow quite large, while males are much smaller, short-lived, and often mistaken for brown recluse spiders due to their similar coloration.

children.description: Crevice weavers are small to medium-sized spiders that build distinctive funnel-shaped webs in cracks, crevices, and small openings in rocks, tree bark, or human structures. These patient hunters sit at the narrow end of their funnel webs, waiting for prey to become entangled in the silky sheets before rushing out to capture their meal. They are typically brown or gray in color, helping them blend in with their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Crevice weavers can be identified by their distinctive web structure - a funnel or tube-shaped retreat connected to a flat sheet web that extends outward from cracks or crevices. Unlike grass spiders which build similar funnel webs in open areas, crevice weavers specifically build their webs in tight spaces and rocky crevices.
children.funFact: Female crevice weavers are known for their longevity, with some species living for several years and continuing to expand and maintain the same web throughout their lives.

children.name: Nephilidae
Trichonephila
children.description: Banded Orbweavers are large, colorful spiders that build impressive golden-yellow webs to catch flying insects. These spiders are known for their distinctive banded leg patterns and relatively large size compared to other orb weavers. They prefer to build their webs in open areas where they can catch plenty of flying prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb weavers, Banded Orbweavers create webs with a distinctive golden or yellowish silk that shimmer in sunlight. Their webs are also notably larger and more robust than typical orb weaver webs.
children.funFact: The Joro Spider, our only New England representative, is actually a recent arrival from East Asia and has been rapidly expanding its range across the eastern United States since around 2013.

children.description: Golden Orbweavers are a family of spiders known for building large, semi-permanent orb webs with golden-colored silk that shimmers in sunlight. These spiders are typically found in warmer climates and create impressive webs that can persist for weeks or months. The females are much larger than males and often allow smaller males to live on their webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orb weaver families, Golden Orbweavers produce distinctively golden or yellowish silk that gives their webs a characteristic metallic sheen. Their webs are also notably large and built to be long-lasting rather than rebuilt daily.
children.funFact: The golden silk produced by these spiders is so strong and lustrous that it has been used to weave actual textiles, including a rare golden cape displayed at the American Museum of Natural History that required silk from over one million Madagascar Golden Orb Weavers.

children.name: Nesticidae
Nesticus
children.description: Nesticus is a genus of small, pale spiders that have adapted to life in caves and other dark, humid environments. These spiders are typically found in underground spaces where they build simple webs to catch small insects and other prey. They have evolved special traits that help them survive in the constant darkness of cave systems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nesticus spiders are characterized by their reduced or absent eyes and pale coloration, adaptations that reflect their cave-dwelling lifestyle. They can be distinguished from other cave spiders by their specific web-building patterns and body structure.
children.funFact: Cave spiders in the genus Nesticus often have such reduced eyesight that they rely almost entirely on vibrations and touch to navigate their dark underground world.

children.description: Cave cobweb spiders are small, pale spiders that have adapted to life in caves, cellars, and other dark, humid places. They build irregular cobwebs to catch tiny prey like springtails and other small arthropods. These spiders are often nearly colorless or yellowish due to their cave-dwelling lifestyle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cobweb spiders, cave cobweb spiders have reduced eyes and lighter coloration as adaptations to their dark underground habitats. They also have longer legs relative to their body size compared to their surface-dwelling relatives.
children.funFact: Cave cobweb spiders can live for several years, which is unusually long for small spiders, likely as an adaptation to the stable but food-scarce cave environment.

children.name: Miturgidae
Zora
children.description: Zora is a genus of small ground-dwelling spiders that are active hunters rather than web builders. These tiny spiders are often found running along the forest floor, under leaf litter, and on low vegetation where they search for small prey like springtails and other tiny insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Zora spiders can be distinguished from other small hunting spiders by their relatively long legs, pale coloration, and their habit of running in short, quick bursts followed by sudden stops.
children.funFact: Despite being less than 3mm long, Zora pumila spiders are excellent jumpers and can leap several times their body length to escape predators or catch prey.

children.description: Prowling spiders are small to medium-sized hunting spiders that actively search for prey rather than building webs to catch food. They are swift runners with excellent eyesight, using their speed and agility to chase down insects and other small arthropods. These spiders are often found on vegetation, tree bark, or leaf litter where they patrol for meals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike web-building spiders, prowling spiders have strong, well-developed legs for running and jumping, and they typically have better vision than their web-spinning relatives. They can be distinguished from wolf spiders by their smaller size and different eye arrangement.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'prowling' spiders, many species in this family are most active during the day, making them some of the few spiders you're likely to see hunting in broad daylight.

children.name: Liocranidae
Agroeca
children.description: Agroeca is a genus of small, ground-dwelling spiders that belong to the family Liocranidae, commonly known as spiny-legged sac spiders. These spiders are typically pale-colored and build silken retreats under stones, logs, or in leaf litter where they rest during the day. They are active nocturnal hunters that prey on small insects and other arthropods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Agroeca can be distinguished from other sac spiders by their relatively robust build and the presence of distinct spines on their legs. They also have a characteristic eye arrangement and tend to be slightly larger than many other liocranid spiders.
children.funFact: Despite being nocturnal hunters, Agroeca spiders are sometimes found wandering during the day in early spring when they emerge from their winter hiding spots to mate.

children.description: Spiny-legged sac spiders are small hunting spiders that get their name from the distinctive spines on their legs. They are active predators that don't build webs to catch prey, instead roaming around to hunt other small arthropods. These spiders create silken retreats or sacs where they rest during the day and lay their eggs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike web-building spiders, these hunters are distinguished by their prominent leg spines and their habit of constructing silk sacs for shelter rather than prey capture. Their robust, spiny legs make them well-equipped for their ground-dwelling lifestyle.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'sac spiders,' they don't actually live in their silk sacs full-time - they use them more like temporary hotels, creating new ones as they move through their territory.

children.name: Zodariidae
Zodarion
children.description: Ant spiders are small, ground-dwelling spiders that have evolved to specialize in hunting ants as their primary prey. These compact spiders are typically dark-colored and move quickly across the ground, often mimicking the movements of their ant prey to get close enough to strike.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most spiders that build webs or ambush various prey, ant spiders are active hunters that specifically target ants and have developed specialized behaviors and body shapes for this lifestyle.
children.funFact: Ant spiders are immune to the formic acid that ants use as a chemical defense, allowing them to safely consume prey that would be toxic to many other predators.

children.description: Ant-eating spiders are a specialized family of small hunting spiders that have evolved specifically to prey on ants. These spiders don't build webs to catch their food, but instead actively hunt and attack ants using specialized behaviors and body features. They are typically small, fast-moving spiders that can be found in areas where ants are abundant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These spiders have hardened, thickened front legs and strong jaws that help them grab and subdue their well-defended ant prey. Their body shape is often compact and robust, adapted for wrestling with ants that might fight back with stings or bites.
children.funFact: Some ant-eating spiders are such convincing mimics that they can walk right into ant colonies undetected, blending in with their prey until they're ready to strike.

children.name: Titanoecidae
Titanoeca
children.description: Titanoeca is a genus of small ground-dwelling spiders that are part of the titanoecid spider family. These spiders are typically found living under stones, logs, and leaf litter where they hunt for small prey rather than building webs to catch food. They are generally dark-colored and well-adapted to life on the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Titanoeca spiders can be distinguished from other ground spiders by their robust build and their unique eye arrangement, with the front row of eyes being distinctly curved. They also have relatively thick legs compared to many other small spider species.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'titanoeca' which sounds quite grand, these are actually quite tiny spiders, usually measuring less than 6mm in length - proving that big names don't always mean big size!

children.description: Rock Weavers are a small family of spiders known for their unique web-building behavior and preference for rocky habitats. These spiders create distinctive flat, sheet-like webs that they weave directly onto rock surfaces, stone walls, and similar hard substrates. They are typically small to medium-sized spiders with robust builds adapted for life in crevices and rocky environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most web-building spiders that construct three-dimensional webs, Rock Weavers create flat, tightly woven sheet webs that lie flush against rock surfaces. They can be distinguished from similar families by their unique spinnerets and the characteristic way they incorporate silk directly into rock crevices.
children.funFact: Rock Weavers got their common name because they literally weave their webs into the texture of rocks, creating some of the flattest spider webs in nature that can be nearly invisible against stone surfaces.

children.description: Spiders are eight-legged predators that belong to the arachnid family, making them relatives of scorpions and ticks rather than insects. All spiders can produce silk from special glands, though they use it in remarkably different ways - from building intricate webs to creating safety lines while hunting. They are exclusively carnivorous, feeding primarily on insects and other small prey that they capture and digest using venom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike insects, spiders have eight legs instead of six, two main body segments instead of three, and no antennae or wings. They are the only animals that can produce multiple types of silk from specialized organs called spinnerets.
children.funFact: Spider silk is stronger than steel by weight and more elastic than rubber - some species can produce up to seven different types of silk for various purposes like web construction, prey wrapping, and creating egg sacs.

children.name: Sarcoptiformes
Eriophyidae
Aceria
children.description: Aceria is a genus of tiny mites that specialize in creating distinctive galls, pouches, and fuzzy growths on leaves, buds, and other plant parts. These microscopic creatures are so small they're barely visible to the naked eye, but their handiwork is often quite noticeable as abnormal growths on trees and shrubs. Each species typically targets a specific type of plant, from oaks and elms to ash trees and walnuts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mites, Aceria species are highly specialized plant modifiers that induce their host plants to form protective structures around them. They have elongated, worm-like bodies with only four legs (instead of the typical eight found in adult mites) and are among the smallest arthropods in New England.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that hundreds could fit on a pinhead, Aceria mites are master architects that can completely redesign plant tissue, turning a normal leaf into a fuzzy carpet of protective hairs or transforming a simple bud into an elaborate gall structure.

children.name: Eriophyes
children.description: Eriophyes is a genus of microscopic mites that are master plant manipulators, causing trees and shrubs to form distinctive galls, blisters, and felt-like growths on their leaves. These tiny arthropods are highly specialized, with each species typically targeting just one type of host plant where they feed and reproduce. You'll often notice their handiwork before you ever see the mites themselves - look for unusual bumps, fuzzy patches, or finger-like projections on leaves throughout New England's forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other plant-feeding mites, Eriophyes species have only two pairs of legs (instead of the typical four pairs) and possess elongated, worm-like bodies perfectly adapted for living inside plant tissues. They're distinguished from other gall-making insects by creating their homes through chemical manipulation of plant growth rather than simply hollowing out existing plant parts.
children.funFact: These mites are so small that hundreds could fit on the head of a pin, yet they can completely reshape a leaf by injecting growth-regulating chemicals that trick the plant into building them custom homes!

children.name: Acalitus
children.description: Acalitus is a genus of tiny mites that are specialized plant parasites, creating distinctive fuzzy growths called erinea on tree leaves. These microscopic creatures are so small they're invisible to the naked eye, yet they can dramatically alter the appearance of leaves by stimulating abnormal hair growth on the leaf surface. Each species typically targets specific tree species, forming a close relationship with their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other plant-feeding mites, Acalitus species create characteristic felt-like patches or blisters on leaves by causing the plant to grow dense clusters of modified hairs. They have extremely elongated, worm-like bodies that are perfectly adapted for living within the plant tissues they modify.
children.funFact: The fuzzy growths these mites create on leaves were once thought to be fungal infections, but they're actually the plant's response to the mites' feeding - essentially tiny 'houses' that the mites trick the tree into building for them!

children.name: Vasates
children.description: Vasates is a genus of microscopic mites that specialize in creating distinctive galls on maple trees. These tiny arachnids live inside the plant tissues they modify, feeding on the tree's fluids while causing the formation of characteristic bumps, blisters, or spindle-shaped growths on maple leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other gall-forming insects, Vasates mites are so small they're nearly invisible to the naked eye, and they create very specific types of galls that are unique to maple trees. Each species in this genus produces its own distinctive gall shape - either spindle-like growths or bladder-shaped blisters.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible without magnification, these tiny mites are master architects that can completely reshape maple leaf tissue to create their own custom living spaces.

children.name: Aculus
children.description: Aculus is a genus of extremely tiny mites that live on plants, so small they're barely visible to the naked eye. These microscopic creatures are plant specialists that feed by piercing plant tissues with their needle-like mouthparts and sucking out cell contents. They're part of the eriophyid mite family, which are among the smallest arthropods on Earth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mites that have four pairs of legs, Aculus mites have only two pairs of legs as adults, giving them a distinctive worm-like appearance. Their elongated, cylindrical bodies are perfectly adapted for living in tight spaces like leaf buds and plant crevices.
children.funFact: Despite being incredibly small (often less than 0.2mm long), some Aculus species can cause dramatic plant galls - abnormal growths that can be hundreds of times larger than the tiny mites that create them!

children.name: Aculops
children.description: Aculops is a genus of extremely tiny mites that specialize in feeding on plant leaves. These microscopic creatures are so small they're barely visible to the naked eye, typically measuring less than 0.2 millimeters long. They use their needle-like mouthparts to pierce plant cells and feed on the contents, often causing distinctive damage patterns on their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Aculops mites have only two pairs of legs instead of the typical four pairs found in most adult mites. They also have elongated, worm-like bodies that are much more streamlined than other mite groups.
children.funFact: The Poison Ivy Leaf Mite found in New England is actually considered beneficial by many people because it feeds exclusively on poison ivy plants, potentially helping to control this troublesome plant naturally!

children.name: Phyllocoptes
children.description: Phyllocoptes is a genus of extremely tiny mites that are specialized plant parasites, measuring less than 0.2 millimeters in length. These microscopic creatures live on the surfaces of leaves and other plant parts, where they feed by piercing plant cells and sucking out the contents. They are part of the larger group of eriophyid mites, which are among the smallest arthropods on Earth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mites that have four pairs of legs, Phyllocoptes mites have only two pairs of legs and elongated, worm-like bodies that help them move through tight spaces on plant surfaces. Their bodies are distinctively segmented and they lack the rounded appearance of typical mites.
children.funFact: Despite being nearly invisible to the naked eye, Phyllocoptes mites can cause significant damage to plants and are important agricultural pests, with some species capable of transmitting plant viruses as they feed.

children.name: Colomerus
children.description: Colomerus is a genus of tiny eriophyid mites that are specialized plant parasites. These microscopic creatures are elongated and worm-like, with only two pairs of legs instead of the typical four pairs found in most mites. They live and feed inside plant tissues, creating distinctive growths and damage on their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mites, Colomerus species have extremely elongated, cylindrical bodies and possess only two pairs of legs located near their front end. They are also distinguished by their ability to induce the formation of abnormal plant growths called erinea, which appear as fuzzy, felt-like patches on leaves.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye at only 0.1-0.2mm long, a single grape leaf can harbor thousands of these mites living within the protective felt-like erinea they create on the leaf surface.

children.name: Cecidophyopsis
children.description: Cecidophyopsis is a genus of tiny eriophyid mites that are highly specialized plant parasites. These microscopic arthropods are known for creating distinctive galls (abnormal growths) on their host plants, where they live and feed on plant tissues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mites, Cecidophyopsis species have elongated, worm-like bodies with only two pairs of legs instead of the typical four pairs found in most adult mites. They are distinguished by their ability to induce specific types of bud galls on woody plants.
children.funFact: These mites are so small that hundreds of them can live inside a single plant bud, causing it to swell into a distinctive rounded gall that can be easily spotted during winter when leaves have fallen.

children.description: Gall and rust mites are microscopic plant parasites that create distinctive growths called galls on leaves, buds, and stems of trees and shrubs. These tiny mites are so small they're invisible to the naked eye, yet they can dramatically alter plant growth by injecting chemicals that cause abnormal tissue development. Many species are highly host-specific, meaning each type of mite typically affects only one or a few closely related plant species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mites that have eight legs, adult eriophyid mites have only four legs and extremely elongated, worm-like bodies. They lack the typical rounded body shape of most mites and are among the smallest arthropods on Earth.
children.funFact: Some gall mites are so tiny that hundreds of them could fit on the head of a pin, yet a single mite can trigger the formation of a gall many thousands of times larger than itself!

children.name: Phytoptidae
Phytoptus
children.description: Phytoptus is a genus of extremely tiny plant mites that are microscopic in size and live exclusively on plants. These mites are so small they can only be seen with magnification, and they spend their entire lives feeding on plant tissues, often causing distinctive galls, blisters, or other deformities on leaves and buds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mites, Phytoptus mites have elongated, worm-like bodies with only two pairs of legs instead of the typical four pairs found in most adult mites. They are highly specialized plant parasites that create species-specific damage patterns on their host plants.
children.funFact: The Filbert Bud Mite can cause hazelnuts to develop 'big bud' disease, where the buds swell to many times their normal size as thousands of mites feed and reproduce inside them.

children.description: Phytoptidae are microscopic mites that are highly specialized plant parasites, living inside plant tissues like leaves, buds, and stems. These tiny arachnids are so small they're barely visible to the naked eye, yet they can cause significant damage to their host plants by feeding on plant cells and creating galls or other deformities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mites, phytoptids have extremely elongated, worm-like bodies with only two pairs of legs (instead of the typical four pairs found in adult mites). Their unique body shape allows them to live within the narrow spaces inside plant tissues.
children.funFact: These mites are so tiny that hundreds of them could fit on the head of a pin, yet they're responsible for creating those peculiar bumps and growths you sometimes see on tree leaves.

children.name: Sarcoptidae
Sarcoptes
children.description: Sarcoptes is a genus of microscopic mites that are obligate parasites, meaning they must live on or in their host to survive. These tiny arachnids burrow into the skin of mammals, creating tunnels where they live, feed, and reproduce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mites that live on the surface or in hair follicles, Sarcoptes mites actually burrow deep into the skin layers of their hosts. They have specialized mouthparts and claws perfectly adapted for digging through skin tissue.
children.funFact: The scabies mite has been a companion to humans for thousands of years - evidence of scabies infections has been found in ancient Egyptian mummies!

children.description: Itch mites are microscopic parasitic arachnids that burrow into the skin of mammals, including humans, causing intense itching and skin irritation. These tiny mites are responsible for the condition known as scabies, where they create tunnels in the outer layer of skin to lay their eggs. They are obligate parasites, meaning they cannot survive for long periods away from their host.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mite families, itch mites have specialized adaptations for burrowing, including strong front legs with claws and a rounded body shape that helps them tunnel through skin layers. They also have distinctive cone-shaped projections called tubercles on their backs.
children.funFact: A female itch mite is so small that 10 of them could fit on the head of a pin, yet she can tunnel through human skin at a rate of 2-3 millimeters per day while laying up to 3 eggs daily!

children.name: Epidermoptidae
Knemidokoptes
children.description: Scaly leg mites are tiny parasitic mites that burrow into the skin of birds, particularly chickens and other poultry. These microscopic creatures live their entire life cycle on their host, feeding on skin cells and keratin while creating tunnels beneath the surface of the skin.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mites, scaly leg mites are highly specialized parasites that burrow deep into the skin rather than living on the surface. They have short, stubby legs and a rounded body shape perfectly adapted for their underground lifestyle.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, these mites can cause the thick, crusty scales that give 'scaly leg' disease its name, making a bird's legs look like they're wearing armor!

children.description: Epidermoptidae is a family of microscopic mites that are specialized parasites living on and within the skin of birds and mammals. These tiny arachnids have evolved to burrow into the skin layers of their hosts, where they feed and complete their life cycles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mite families, epidermoptid mites have highly reduced legs and bodies specifically adapted for living within the skin layers of their hosts. They create characteristic tunnels and burrows in the skin, particularly affecting the legs and feet of birds.
children.funFact: The scaly leg mites in this family can cause the characteristic 'scaly leg' condition in chickens and other birds, where the legs become thick and crusty due to the mites burrowing under the scales.

children.description: Sarcoptiformes are tiny mites that have adapted to live in very close association with plants and animals. Most are so small they're invisible to the naked eye, yet they play important roles as both plant feeders and parasites. These microscopic arachnids include some that cause plant galls and others that burrow into skin.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mites, members of this group have lost their breathing tubes (tracheae) and breathe directly through their skin. They also tend to have simplified body structures adapted for their specialized lifestyles.
children.funFact: Some gall mites in this group are so tiny that hundreds could fit on the head of a pin, yet they're capable of completely transforming the growth of plant tissues to create their own custom homes!

children.name: Opiliones
Sclerosomatidae
Leiobunum
children.description: Leiobunum harvestmen are the gangly-legged arachnids you'll often spot scurrying across walls, tree trunks, or leaf litter throughout New England. These 'daddy longlegs' are characterized by their extremely long, thin legs that can be many times longer than their small, oval bodies. Unlike spiders, they have a single, fused body segment and cannot produce silk or venom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Leiobunum species typically have exceptionally long, slender legs relative to other harvestman genera, and their bodies are usually smooth and relatively small. Many species in this genus also have distinctive eye bumps (ocularia) and specific patterns of spines or tubercles on their legs.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, Leiobunum harvestmen are actually quite hardy and can regenerate lost legs, though the new leg will be shorter than the original - a useful adaptation when escaping predators by sacrificing a limb!

children.name: Nelima
children.description: Nelima is a genus of harvestmen, also known as daddy longlegs, that are commonly found throughout New England's forests and gardens. These arachnids have extremely long, thin legs that can span several inches, and small oval bodies that are typically brown or gray in color. Unlike spiders, harvestmen have their body segments fused together and do not produce silk or venom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nelima species can be distinguished from other harvestmen by their particularly long legs relative to their body size and their tendency to form large aggregations. They also have distinctive eye arrangements and body patterns that help separate them from similar-looking genera.
children.funFact: Nelima harvestmen are known for their unusual defensive behavior of vibrating rapidly when threatened, causing their entire body to blur and potentially confuse predators.

children.name: Hadrobunus
children.description: Hadrobunus is a genus of harvestmen, also known as daddy longlegs, that are arachnids related to spiders but with some key differences. These creatures have extremely long, thin legs relative to their small oval bodies and don't produce silk or venom like spiders do. They are predators and scavengers that hunt for small insects and other tiny prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hadrobunus harvestmen can be distinguished from other harvestman genera by their relatively robust body structure and distinctive leg proportions. They also have characteristic markings and coloration patterns that help separate them from closely related groups.
children.funFact: Unlike spiders, harvestmen like those in the genus Hadrobunus can detach their legs when grabbed by predators - the detached leg continues to twitch and move, distracting the predator while the harvestman escapes!

children.description: Sclerosomatid harvestmen are a family of daddy longlegs known for their extremely long, thin legs that can span several times their body length. These arachnids have oval-shaped bodies and are commonly found in gardens, forests, and around human dwellings throughout New England. Unlike spiders, they cannot produce silk and typically feed on small insects, decaying organic matter, and plant juices.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sclerosomatid harvestmen can be distinguished from other harvestman families by their relatively soft bodies and the way their legs easily detach when grabbed by predators. They also tend to have longer legs relative to their body size compared to most other harvestman groups.
children.funFact: When threatened, these harvestmen can intentionally shed their legs through a process called autotomy - the detached leg will continue to twitch for several minutes, distracting predators while the harvestman escapes!

children.name: Phalangiidae
Odiellus
children.description: Odiellus is a genus of harvestmen, also known as daddy longlegs, that are common arachnids found throughout New England. These small creatures have oval-shaped bodies and extremely long, thin legs that they use to navigate through leaf litter, under rocks, and in other moist habitats. Unlike spiders, harvestmen don't produce silk or venom, and they're completely harmless to humans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the Odiellus genus can be identified by their relatively robust bodies compared to other harvestmen, and many species have distinctive color patterns or markings on their backs. They also tend to have shorter legs relative to their body size compared to some other harvestman genera.
children.funFact: When threatened, Odiellus harvestmen can detach their legs as a defense mechanism - the detached leg will continue to twitch for several minutes, potentially distracting predators while the harvestman escapes!

children.name: Phalangium
children.description: Phalangium is a genus of harvestmen, those long-legged arachnids often mistaken for spiders but lacking the ability to produce silk or venom. These creatures are characterized by their compact, oval-shaped bodies and exceptionally long, thin legs that can span several times their body length. They're typically found scurrying across garden walls, tree trunks, and rocky surfaces throughout temperate regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Phalangium can be distinguished from other harvestmen by their relatively smooth, rounded bodies and the specific pattern of spines and tubercles on their legs and body segments. Unlike many harvestmen that are secretive, Phalangium species are often active during daylight hours.
children.funFact: The European Harvestman can detach its legs when grabbed by a predator, and the detached leg will continue to twitch for several minutes, distracting the predator while the harvestman escapes - though unlike lizards, they cannot regrow lost legs.

children.name: Rilaena
children.description: Rilaena is a small genus of harvestmen, which are arachnids that look like spiders but have their body segments fused together into what appears to be a single oval shape. These creatures are part of the diverse world of daddy longlegs, though they're quite different from the more familiar long-legged species most people know. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species that emerges in spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Rilaena are distinguished by their relatively compact body shape and shorter legs compared to many other harvestmen. They have a distinctive triangular or wedge-shaped appearance when viewed from above.
children.funFact: The Spring Harvestman gets its name because it's one of the few harvestmen species that's most active in spring rather than fall, making it a delightful early-season discovery for nature explorers.

children.name: Oligolophus
children.description: Oligolophus is a genus of harvestmen, also known as daddy longlegs, which are arachnids related to spiders but with some key differences. These creatures have extremely long, thin legs relative to their small, oval-shaped bodies and cannot produce silk or venom like true spiders. They are typically found in moist environments like forests, gardens, and caves where they hunt for small insects and decomposing organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Oligolophus can be distinguished from other harvestmen by their relatively robust body structure and specific arrangements of spines and bumps on their body segments. They also tend to have shorter legs compared to some other daddy longlegs species.
children.funFact: Despite their spider-like appearance, harvestmen in the genus Oligolophus have been around for over 400 million years, making them some of the most ancient arachnids on Earth!

children.name: Mitopus
children.description: Mitopus is a genus of harvestmen (also called daddy longlegs) that are characterized by their distinctive body markings and relatively robust build compared to other harvestmen. These arachnids have oval-shaped bodies and long, thin legs that they use to navigate through leaf litter and low vegetation in search of small prey and decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Mitopus can be distinguished from other harvestmen by their distinctive saddle-shaped marking on the back of their body, which gives the Saddleback Harvestman its common name. They also tend to have shorter, sturdier legs relative to their body size compared to many other harvestman species.
children.funFact: Despite being called daddy longlegs like spiders, harvestmen in the genus Mitopus cannot produce silk or venom, and unlike spiders, their body segments are fused together into what appears to be a single oval unit.

children.description: Phalangiid harvestmen are the classic "daddy longlegs" that many people recognize, with extremely long, thin legs and small oval bodies. These arachnids are commonly found in gardens, forests, and around homes throughout New England, where they hunt small insects and scavenge organic matter. Unlike spiders, they have a single body segment and cannot produce silk or venom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phalangiid harvestmen can be distinguished from other harvestman families by their relatively smooth bodies and the way their eyes are positioned on a small raised bump called an ocularium. Their legs are typically much longer in proportion to their body size compared to most other harvestman groups.
children.funFact: When threatened, phalangiid harvestmen can deliberately shed one of their legs, which continues to twitch for several minutes to distract predators while the harvestman escapes - but unlike some other animals, the leg never grows back.

children.name: Caddidae
Caddo
children.description: Caddo is a small genus of tiny sheet weaver spiders that build delicate horizontal webs close to the ground. These diminutive spiders are commonly found in leaf litter, under logs, and in other moist woodland habitats where they hunt for small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Caddo spiders can be distinguished from other sheet weavers by their extremely small size and their tendency to build webs very close to or on the ground surface, rather than elevated between vegetation.
children.funFact: Despite being among the smallest spiders in New England, Caddo spiders are incredibly active hunters that can quickly dart across their sheet webs to capture prey much larger than themselves.

children.description: Large-eyed Harvestmen are a small family of arachnids that, as their name suggests, are distinguished by their notably large eyes compared to other harvestmen species. These delicate, long-legged creatures are part of the diverse order of harvestmen, which are often mistaken for spiders but are actually quite different. They typically have small, oval bodies and extremely long, thin legs that they use to navigate through leaf litter and low vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their most obvious feature is their proportionally large eyes, which are much more prominent than those found in most other harvestmen families. They also tend to have more delicate body structures and longer legs relative to their body size.
children.funFact: Despite having such large eyes, harvestmen actually have relatively poor vision and rely more on vibrations and chemical signals to navigate their world and find food.

children.name: Trogulidae
Trogulus
children.description: Trogulus is a genus of harvestmen (also called daddy longlegs) that are among the most unusual-looking arachnids you might encounter. These creatures have extremely flattened, armor-like bodies that make them look almost like tiny shields with legs, and they're perfectly adapted for hiding under rocks and in crevices.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical harvestmen with their round bodies and long thin legs, Trogulus species have remarkably flattened, heavily armored bodies that are wider than they are tall. Their legs are also shorter and sturdier compared to other harvestmen.
children.funFact: When threatened, these "armored harvestmen" can press their flat bodies tightly against rock surfaces, becoming nearly invisible and almost impossible to pry loose.

children.description: Trogulid harvestmen are small, armored-looking arachnids that are easily mistaken for tiny beetles or mites. These secretive creatures have distinctively flattened, heavily sclerotized (hardened) bodies that help them squeeze into tight spaces under rocks, logs, and leaf litter. They are among the most primitive harvestmen families, with ancient origins dating back millions of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical harvestmen with their long, spindly legs, trogulids have relatively short legs and remarkably flattened, turtle-like bodies covered in hard plates. Their body shape and armor-like appearance make them unmistakable among New England's arachnids.
children.funFact: Trogulid harvestmen are so flattened they can slip through cracks barely thicker than a sheet of paper, earning them the nickname 'pancake harvestmen.'

children.name: Nemastomatidae
Nemastoma
children.description: Nemastoma is a genus of small harvestmen (also called daddy longlegs) that are part of the arachnid family.
