These creatures are characterized by their compact, rounded bodies and relatively short legs compared to other harvestmen. They are typically found in leaf litter and under logs in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike the more familiar long-legged harvestmen, Nemastoma species have notably shorter legs and more robust, oval-shaped bodies. They also have distinctive eye arrangements and feeding structures that set them apart from other harvestman genera.
children.funFact: Despite being called daddy longlegs, Nemastoma harvestmen actually have some of the shortest legs relative to body size among all harvestmen species!

children.description: Nemastomatid harvestmen are a family of small, delicate arachnids that look like tiny spiders with extremely long, thin legs. Unlike true spiders, these harvestmen have their body segments fused together and cannot produce silk or venom. They are secretive creatures that prefer moist, hidden environments like leaf litter and under logs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These harvestmen can be distinguished from other harvestman families by their relatively small size and the presence of scent glands that can produce defensive chemicals when threatened. They also have distinctive eye arrangements and body proportions that set them apart from their relatives.
children.funFact: When threatened, nemastomatid harvestmen can release foul-smelling chemicals from special glands, earning some species the nickname 'stink daddies' - though they're completely harmless to humans!

children.name: Sabaconidae
Sabacon
children.description: Sabacon is a genus of harvestmen (also called daddy longlegs) that are specialized for life in caves and other dark, humid environments. These arachnids have extremely long, thin legs and small bodies, making them well-adapted for navigating tight spaces in underground habitats. They are part of the opilionid family and are considered living fossils, representing an ancient lineage of harvestmen.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sabacon harvestmen are distinguished from other harvestmen by their cave-dwelling lifestyle and their exceptionally long, delicate legs relative to their tiny body size. They also have reduced eyesight compared to surface-dwelling relatives, reflecting their adaptation to dark environments.
children.funFact: Sabacon harvestmen are so ancient that they're sometimes called 'living fossils' - fossils of very similar species have been found in 50-million-year-old amber, showing they've barely changed over geological time!

children.description: Sabaconid harvestmen are a small family of arachnids that belong to the order of harvestmen (also called daddy longlegs). These creatures have extremely long, thin legs and small oval bodies, and are known for their secretive lifestyle in moist forest environments. Unlike spiders, harvestmen cannot produce silk and are generally harmless scavengers that feed on small insects and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sabaconid harvestmen are distinguished from other harvestmen families by their unique body structure, including specialized leg segments and distinctive reproductive organs. They tend to be smaller and more delicate than many other harvestmen species.
children.funFact: The single New England species of sabaconid harvestmen is so rare and elusive that it's considered one of the most difficult arachnids to find in the region, often hiding deep in leaf litter and emerging only at night.

children.description: Harvestmen, also known as daddy longlegs, are arachnids with extremely long, thin legs and compact, oval-shaped bodies. Unlike spiders, their body appears to be all one piece since their abdomen and cephalothorax are broadly joined together. These gentle creatures are commonly found scurrying across forest floors, walls, and vegetation throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Harvestmen can be distinguished from spiders by their fused body segments that create a single oval shape, and they have only two eyes mounted on a small turret-like structure. Unlike spiders, they cannot produce silk and do not have fangs or venom.
children.funFact: Despite their nickname 'daddy longlegs,' harvestmen are completely harmless to humans and will often gather in large groups during the day, creating wiggling masses of dozens of individuals that may help them stay moist and avoid predators.

children.name: Trombidiformes
Tetranychidae
Eurytetranychus
children.description: Eurytetranychus is a genus of spider mites that are tiny plant-feeding arachnids barely visible to the naked eye. These microscopic creatures are specialized plant parasites that pierce plant cells with their needle-like mouthparts to feed on cell contents, often causing stippling or yellowing of leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other spider mites by their specific body proportions and the arrangement of their defensive bristles (setae). They typically have a more elongated body shape compared to many other tetranychid mites.
children.funFact: Despite being only about 0.4 millimeters long, boxwood mites can cause significant damage to ornamental plants and are considered important horticultural pests in landscaping.

children.name: Petrobia
children.description: Petrobia is a genus of tiny spider mites that are plant-feeding arachnids, not true insects. These microscopic creatures are so small they're barely visible to the naked eye, typically appearing as moving specks on plant surfaces. They use their needle-like mouthparts to pierce plant cells and feed on the contents.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Petrobia mites are distinguished from other spider mites by their preference for feeding on herbaceous plants like woodsorrel and their ability to survive in cooler temperatures than many related species.
children.funFact: Despite being called the Woodsorrel Mite, Petrobia harti can actually feed on over 60 different plant species, making it quite the generalist feeder in the spider mite world.

children.name: Tetranychus
children.description: Tetranychus is a genus of tiny spider mites that are among the most economically important plant pests worldwide. These microscopic arachnids are plant feeders that use their needle-like mouthparts to pierce plant cells and suck out the contents, often causing significant damage to crops and garden plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their extremely small size (less than 1mm), ability to produce fine webbing on infested plants, and their tendency to feed in large colonies on the undersides of leaves.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'spider mites,' these creatures are so small that a period at the end of a sentence could hide about 100 of them!

children.name: Bryobia
children.description: Bryobia is a genus of tiny spider mites that are commonly found crawling on plants and around homes. These microscopic arachnids are plant feeders that use their needle-like mouthparts to pierce plant cells and suck out the contents. Despite their small size, they can sometimes be seen as tiny moving dots, especially on sunny days.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bryobia mites are distinguished from other spider mites by their longer front legs and reddish-brown coloration. They also tend to be slightly larger than many other plant-feeding mites.
children.funFact: Clover mites often invade homes in large numbers during spring and fall, but they're completely harmless to humans and actually can't survive indoors for long because they need plant food to live.

children.name: Oligonychus
children.description: Oligonychus is a genus of tiny spider mites that are specialized plant-feeders, using their needle-like mouthparts to pierce plant cells and suck out the contents. These microscopic arachnids are closely related to spiders and ticks, but have adapted to life as plant parasites. In New England, this genus is represented by the Spruce Spider Mite, which specifically targets coniferous trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Oligonychus can be distinguished from other spider mites by their preference for coniferous hosts and their ability to produce fine webbing on needle-bearing trees. They typically cause yellowing or bronzing of pine and spruce needles rather than the leaf stippling seen with other spider mite genera.
children.funFact: Despite being barely visible to the naked eye, a single Spruce Spider Mite can lay up to 100 eggs in its lifetime, allowing populations to explode rapidly during hot, dry conditions.

children.description: Spider mites are tiny plant-feeding arachnids that belong to the same group as spiders and ticks. These microscopic creatures live on the undersides of leaves where they pierce plant cells and feed on the contents, often creating fine webbing similar to spider silk. Most are so small they're barely visible to the naked eye, typically measuring less than 1mm in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mites, spider mites have specialized mouthparts for piercing plant cells and most species produce fine silk webbing on their host plants. They also have distinctive body shapes that are more oval and flattened compared to other plant-feeding mites.
children.funFact: Some spider mites can reproduce so rapidly that a single female can produce over 100 offspring in just a few weeks, which is why they can suddenly appear to 'explode' in population during hot, dry weather.

children.name: Limnocharidae
Limnochares
children.description: Limnochares is a genus of freshwater mites that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These tiny arachnids are typically bright red or orange in color and are active predators that hunt other small aquatic creatures like water fleas and mosquito larvae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other water mites, Limnochares species have distinctively large, prominent eyes and relatively long legs that help them swim efficiently through the water column rather than just crawling along the bottom.
children.funFact: Despite being only 2-4 millimeters long, these little red mites are voracious hunters that can consume prey nearly as large as themselves!

children.description: Limnocharidae are a family of water mites that live in freshwater habitats like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These tiny arachnids are aquatic throughout their lives, swimming through the water column and crawling along submerged surfaces. They are predators that hunt other small aquatic invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other water mites that are flattened or have specialized swimming hairs, Limnocharidae have relatively round, balloon-like bodies and move through the water with a distinctive wobbling motion.
children.funFact: These water mites are excellent swimmers despite their chunky appearance, using their legs like tiny oars to propel themselves through the water in search of prey.

children.name: Penthaleidae
Penthaleus
children.description: Penthaleus is a genus of tiny predatory mites that are active during cool weather, typically in fall, winter, and early spring. These microscopic arachnids are beneficial garden inhabitants that hunt other small mites and insects. They're part of the velvet mite family and are among the few mites that remain active in cold temperatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mites, Penthaleus species are active in cold weather when other mites are dormant. They have a distinctive dark coloration and are larger than many plant-feeding mites they prey upon.
children.funFact: The Blue Oat Mite gets its name from its bluish-black color and its habit of being found on oat crops, though it's actually a beneficial predator rather than a plant pest.

children.description: Penthaleidae is a small family of mites commonly known as winter grain mites or redlegged earth mites. These tiny arachnids are plant feeders that are most active during cool, moist conditions and can sometimes be seen crawling on soil surfaces or low vegetation. They are among the larger predatory mites, though still quite small to the human eye.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These mites can be distinguished from other soil mites by their relatively large size, reddish-orange coloration, and distinctively long legs. They have a more robust body shape compared to many other plant-feeding mites.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, winter grain mites can sometimes appear in such large numbers on soil surfaces during cool weather that they create visible reddish patches on the ground.

children.name: Bdellidae
Neomolgus
children.description: Neomolgus is a small genus of parasitic copepods that live on marine fish and other sea creatures. These tiny crustaceans are specialized for attaching to their hosts and feeding on their body fluids or tissues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their highly modified body structure adapted for parasitic life, including specialized attachment organs and reduced swimming appendages compared to free-living copepods.
children.funFact: Despite being parasites, these copepods play an important role in marine ecosystems and can actually help scientists monitor the health of fish populations.

children.description: Snout mites are tiny predatory arachnids that get their name from their distinctive elongated mouthparts that form a prominent snout-like projection. These microscopic hunters live in soil, leaf litter, and moss where they actively search for even smaller prey like springtails, other mites, and tiny insects. They are fast-moving predators that use their specialized mouthparts to capture and feed on their victims.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The prominent snout-like extension of their mouthparts makes them easily recognizable among mites. Unlike many other soil-dwelling mites, they are active predators rather than scavengers or plant feeders.
children.funFact: Despite being smaller than a pinhead, snout mites are fierce predators that can move surprisingly quickly through the soil ecosystem, earning them the nickname 'cheetahs of the microscopic world.'

children.name: Demodecidae
Demodex
children.description: Mammalian Follicle Mites are microscopic mites that live exclusively in the hair follicles and oil glands of mammals. These tiny arachnids spend their entire lives burrowing in the skin, feeding on dead skin cells and oils produced by their hosts. They are found on nearly all adult humans and many other mammal species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mites, Demodex species have extremely elongated, worm-like bodies that are perfectly adapted for living in narrow hair follicles. Their legs are reduced to tiny stubs, making them poor at moving outside their follicle homes.
children.funFact: You almost certainly have millions of these mites living on your face right now - they're most active at night when they crawl between follicles to mate!

children.description: Mammalian Follicle Mites are microscopic arachnids that live exclusively in the hair follicles and oil glands of mammals. These tiny eight-legged creatures are so small they can only be seen under a microscope, and they spend their entire lives burrowing within their host's skin.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mites that live on the surface of skin or in the environment, follicle mites have evolved elongated, worm-like bodies perfectly adapted for living deep inside narrow hair follicles.
children.funFact: Nearly every adult human on Earth carries these mites on their face - they're completely harmless and have been living with humans for so long that different human populations around the world have their own distinct varieties of face mites!

children.name: Cheyletiellidae
Cheyletiella
children.description: Cheyletiella is a genus of tiny parasitic mites that live on the skin and in the fur of mammals, including cats, dogs, and rabbits. These microscopic creatures are commonly known as 'walking dandruff' because they appear as moving white specks on their host's fur. They feed on skin cells and tissue fluids, causing itchy skin conditions in both pets and humans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mites that burrow into skin, Cheyletiella mites live on the surface of their host's skin and are large enough to be seen moving with the naked eye or a magnifying glass.
children.funFact: These mites earned the nickname 'walking dandruff' because they're just large enough to see crawling around on fur, looking like tiny moving flakes of dandruff to the naked eye.

children.description: Cheyletiellidae are tiny predatory mites commonly known as 'walking dandruff' mites because they can appear as moving white specks on the skin and fur of mammals. These microscopic arachnids are parasites that feed on skin cells, tissue fluids, and other mites found on their hosts. They're most commonly encountered on rabbits, cats, dogs, and occasionally humans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mite families, Cheyletiellidae have prominent hook-like claws (chelicerae) that give them their name, and they're large enough to be visible to the naked eye as tiny moving dots. They also have a distinctive oval body shape and don't burrow into the skin like scabies mites.
children.funFact: These mites got their nickname 'walking dandruff' because they're just barely visible to the naked eye and create the illusion of dandruff that moves around on their host's fur or skin.

children.description: Trombidiform mites are a diverse group of tiny arachnids that includes both free-living and parasitic species. They can be found in nearly every habitat imaginable, from soil and leaf litter to the hair follicles of mammals, and even in freshwater environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These mites are characterized by their unique respiratory system, with breathing openings located near or on their mouthparts rather than on their body segments like other mite groups.
children.funFact: Some trombidiform mites are so small that entire populations can live undetected in the hair follicles of mammals, including humans, where they feed on dead skin cells and oils.

children.name: Ixodida
Ixodidae
Dermacentor
children.description: Dog ticks are hard-bodied ticks that are common parasites of mammals throughout New England. These ticks have ornate patterns on their backs and are known for their ability to transmit diseases to both animals and humans. They go through complex life cycles involving multiple hosts and can survive for long periods without feeding.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dog ticks are distinguished from other tick genera by their ornate dorsal patterns with white or silver markings, and their rectangular basis capituli (the base of their mouthparts). They are generally larger and more robust than many other tick species when fully engorged.
children.funFact: The American Dog Tick can survive without a blood meal for over two years, waiting patiently on vegetation for a suitable host to pass by.

children.name: Ixodes
children.description: Ixodes is a genus of hard-bodied ticks that are important disease vectors in New England. These small arachnids have a complex three-stage life cycle and feed on blood from mammals, birds, and other vertebrates. They are commonly found in wooded areas and tall grass where they wait to attach to passing hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ixodes ticks can be distinguished from other tick genera by their distinctive shield-like scutum that covers only part of their back, and their long, sword-shaped mouthparts. Unlike some other ticks, they lack ornate patterns or festoons around their body margins.
children.funFact: The Eastern Black-legged Tick can take up to two years to complete its full life cycle, spending most of that time waiting in leaf litter for the perfect moment to find a host.

children.name: Amblyomma
children.description: Bont ticks are a genus of hard ticks known for their distinctive ornate patterns and markings on their backs. These ticks are aggressive blood-feeders that attach to mammals, birds, and reptiles, and are important disease vectors in many regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bont ticks are distinguished from other tick genera by their decorative, often colorful patterns and markings on their scutum (hard back plate), giving them their 'bont' name which means 'colorful' in Afrikaans.
children.funFact: The Lone Star Tick gets its name from the distinctive white or yellowish spot on the back of adult females, resembling the lone star on the Texas flag.

children.name: Haemaphysalis
children.description: Haemaphysalis ticks are small, hard-bodied parasites that feed on the blood of mammals, birds, and reptiles. These ticks have a three-stage life cycle and can survive for long periods without feeding, making them highly adaptable to different environments and host animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their relatively small size compared to other hard ticks, and their mouthparts are shorter than those of common dog ticks or deer ticks.
children.funFact: The Asian Longhorned Tick can reproduce without mating through a process called parthenogenesis, allowing a single female to establish an entire population on her own.

children.name: Rhipicephalus
children.description: Pepper Ticks are a genus of hard-bodied ticks that are important parasites of mammals worldwide. These small arachnids have a three-host life cycle, meaning they feed on different animals during their larval, nymphal, and adult stages. They are known for their ability to transmit various diseases to both animals and humans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other tick genera, Pepper Ticks typically have a more rounded body shape and distinctive coloration patterns. They are also notable for their preference for warmer climates and indoor environments compared to most other tick species.
children.funFact: The Brown Dog Tick is unusual among ticks because it can complete its entire life cycle indoors, making it one of the few tick species that can establish year-round populations inside homes and kennels.

children.description: Hardbacked ticks are parasitic arachnids with tough, shield-like plates covering their backs that give them their common name. These blood-feeding creatures attach to mammals, birds, and reptiles, using specialized mouthparts to pierce skin and feed for days or weeks at a time. All members of this family go through similar life stages - egg, larva, nymph, and adult - with each stage requiring a blood meal to develop further.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike soft ticks, hardbacked ticks have a prominent hard shield (scutum) on their back that's visible even when they're not feeding. They also have forward-projecting mouthparts that are easily seen from above, whereas soft ticks have mouthparts positioned underneath their bodies.
children.funFact: A single female hardbacked tick can lay up to 3,000 eggs after just one blood meal, but the entire life cycle from egg to adult can take anywhere from one to three years to complete.

children.description: Ticks are small, blood-sucking arachnids that are closely related to spiders and mites. They have specialized mouthparts for piercing skin and feeding on the blood of mammals, birds, and other animals. All ticks go through multiple life stages and require blood meals to develop and reproduce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other arachnids, ticks have a specialized feeding apparatus called a capitulum with barbed mouthparts that anchor firmly into their host's skin. Their bodies are also uniquely designed to expand dramatically when engorged with blood.
children.funFact: A tick can increase its body weight by 100 times or more during a single blood meal, transforming from a tiny, flat creature into a plump, grape-sized bloodbag.

children.name: Pseudoscorpiones
Cheliferidae
Chelifer
children.description: Chelifer is a genus of pseudoscorpions, tiny arachnids that look like miniature scorpions but lack the long tail and stinger. These small predators have prominent pincers (called pedipalps) that they use to catch prey like mites, small flies, and other tiny arthropods. They are beneficial creatures that help control pest populations in homes and other buildings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the genus Chelifer are distinguished by their relatively large size among pseudoscorpions and their tendency to live in human-made structures rather than purely natural habitats.
children.funFact: House pseudoscorpions in this genus are sometimes called 'book scorpions' because they were historically found living between the pages of old books, where they fed on book lice and other paper-eating pests.

children.description: Cheliferidae is a family of pseudoscorpions, tiny arachnids that look like miniature scorpions but lack the long tail and stinger. These small predators have prominent pincers (chelae) that they use to catch and hold prey like mites, small insects, and other tiny arthropods. They are beneficial creatures that help control pest populations in leaf litter, under bark, and in soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished from other pseudoscorpions by their relatively large, robust pincers and their preference for living in drier habitats like under tree bark and in wood crevices, rather than in moist soil or leaf litter.
children.funFact: Despite being called pseudoscorpions, these tiny arachnids actually produce silk from glands in their jaws, which they use to build small shelters for molting and overwintering.

children.name: Pseudogarypidae
Pseudogarypus
children.description: Pseudogarypus is a genus of pseudoscorpions, tiny arachnids that look like miniature scorpions but lack the long tail and stinger. These small predators have large pincers (chelae) that they use to catch even smaller prey like mites, springtails, and other tiny invertebrates. They live secretive lives in leaf litter, under bark, and in soil where they hunt for food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Pseudogarypus can be distinguished from other pseudoscorpion genera by their specific arrangement of sensory hairs on their pincers and the structure of their reproductive organs. They tend to be relatively robust compared to some other pseudoscorpion groups.
children.funFact: Despite being called pseudoscorpions, these tiny arachnids are actually beneficial predators that help control populations of even smaller pests, and some species can walk backwards as easily as they walk forwards using their sensitive pincers to feel their way.

children.description: Pseudogarypid pseudoscorpions are tiny arachnids that look like miniature scorpions but lack the long tail and stinger. They have large pincers (chelae) on their front appendages and typically live in leaf litter, under bark, or in soil where they hunt even smaller invertebrates. Despite their fearsome appearance, they are completely harmless to humans and are actually beneficial predators in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished from other pseudoscorpions by their relatively large size and robust build, along with specific arrangements of sensory structures on their pincers. They also have a distinctive pattern of plates (tergites) on their back segments.
children.funFact: Pseudogarypid pseudoscorpions are sometimes called "book scorpions" because they were historically found living between the pages of old books, where they fed on book lice and other tiny pests that damaged paper and bindings.

children.name: Neobisiidae
Microbisium
children.description: Microbisium is a genus of tiny pseudoscorpions, which are small arachnids that look like miniature scorpions but lack the long tail and stinger. These microscopic predators have pincers (chelae) at the front of their bodies that they use to catch even smaller prey like mites, springtails, and other tiny arthropods. They live in leaf litter, soil, and other moist ground habitats where they hunt for food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Microbisium are distinguished from other pseudoscorpions by their extremely small size and specific arrangements of body segments and pincer structures. They have a relatively broad body shape compared to their tiny overall size.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, Microbisium pseudoscorpions are fierce predators in the miniature world of soil organisms, using venom in their pincers to subdue prey that may be nearly as large as themselves.

children.description: Neobisiid pseudoscorpions are tiny arachnids that look like miniature scorpions but lack the long tail and stinger. These small predators have pincers (chelae) for catching prey and are commonly found in soil, leaf litter, and under rocks where they hunt even smaller invertebrates. Despite their scorpion-like appearance, they are completely harmless to humans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Neobisiid pseudoscorpions can be distinguished from other pseudoscorpion families by their specific arrangement of sensory hairs on their pincers and the structure of their chelicerae (mouthparts). They typically have a more elongated body shape compared to some other pseudoscorpion families.
children.funFact: Some neobisiid pseudoscorpions practice a form of hitchhiking called phoresy, where they grab onto flying insects with their pincers to travel to new locations - imagine a tiny arachnid taking a free ride on a beetle!

children.description: Pseudoscorpions are tiny arachnids that look like miniature scorpions but lack the long tail and stinger. These small predators have pincers (chelae) at the front of their bodies that they use to catch and subdue prey like mites, springtails, and other small arthropods. They're found in leaf litter, under bark, in soil, and sometimes even in houses where they hunt for tiny pests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true scorpions, pseudoscorpions have no tail or stinger, and unlike spiders, they have prominent pincers instead of fangs. They're much smaller than true scorpions, typically measuring only 2-8 millimeters in length.
children.funFact: Pseudoscorpions can hitch rides on larger insects like flies and beetles in a behavior called phoresy, using their pincers to grab onto their unwitting taxi for transportation to new hunting grounds.

children.name: Mesostigmata
Laelapidae
Varroa
children.description: Varroa mites are tiny parasitic arachnids that specifically target honey bees and their colonies. These microscopic creatures attach themselves to adult bees and their developing larvae, feeding on their body fluids and weakening entire hives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mites, Varroa mites have evolved to be perfectly sized and shaped to hide between the segments of a bee's body, making them nearly invisible to the naked eye.
children.funFact: A single Varroa mite can reproduce entirely within a bee cell, with one female mite potentially producing 4-5 offspring before the bee emerges from its cell.

children.description: Laelapidae is a large family of predatory mites that are typically found in soil, leaf litter, and as parasites on various animals. Most species in this family are beneficial predators that help control pest insects and other small arthropods, though some have evolved to become parasites of mammals, birds, and insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These mites have well-developed chelicerae (mouthparts) adapted for piercing and a distinctive dorsal shield that covers much of their back. They typically have strong, clawed legs that help them move quickly through their environment.
children.funFact: The infamous Varroa mite, which has devastated honeybee colonies worldwide, belongs to this family despite most of its relatives being helpful predators rather than harmful parasites.

children.description: Mesostigs are a large order of mites that are primarily predators and parasites, living in soil, leaf litter, on plants, or on other animals. They have specialized breathing structures called spiracles located on the sides of their bodies, which help distinguish them from other mite groups. These tiny arachnids play important roles as both hunters of smaller organisms and as parasites of larger animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mesostigs can be identified by their spiracles (breathing pores) positioned on the lateral sides of their body, typically near the second or third pair of legs. They also have a distinctive shield-like plate covering the back portion of their body.
children.funFact: Some mesostig mites are so specialized as parasites that they live exclusively in the nasal passages of seals and other marine mammals, riding along as their hosts dive to incredible depths in the ocean.
